articles.title: Oakland Sheriff investigating bicycle crash that killed former state rep
articles.description: Preliminary reports indicate John Reilly was riding a bicycle Wednesday morning when he hit a bypass pipe that stretched across a pedestrian walkway.
articles.content: Former State Representative John Reilly (R-Oakland Township) pictured in 2020. (Michigan House Republicans)The Oakland County Sheriff is investigating the circumstances of a crash that killed former State Representative John Reilly this week.The sheriff's office said it's looking at factors that could've contributed to his death. In a statement, the office said preliminary reports indicate Reilly was riding a bicycle early Wednesday morning when he hit a bypass pipe that stretched across a pedestrian walkway.The Oakland County Water Resources Commission said in a statement Friday afternoon the pipe was part of one of its sewer projects.“We are grateful to the citizens and first responders who immediately took action to provide lifesaving care," Sheriff Michael Bouchard said. "Our Crash Reconstruction Unit is conducting a thorough investigation to determine the circumstances surrounding this tragedy and provide answers to the many questions it has understandably raised.”Reilly served in the Michigan House of Representatives for six years as a Republican from Oakland County.

Good Truckin’ parks at long-awaited REO Town location
articles.description: After months of anticipation, the once-empty storefront at 1107 S. Washington Ave. in REO Town is serving up the eclectic menu locals missed – Good Truckin’ is back. Good Truckin’ […]
articles.content: After months of anticipation, the once-empty storefront at 1107 S. Washington Ave. in REO Town is serving up the eclectic menu locals missed – Good Truckin’ is back. Good Truckin’ REO Bites is a smaller, grab-and-go version of the Good Truckin’ Diner in Old Town. It is located in the same space the diner occupied until almost two years ago. When the diner moved into a bigger location at the end of 2024, REO Bites was intended to open shortly after. “We were doing our best to get it open,” Nora Gorman said. “We would work on it for two weeks solid, and then stuff would come up with other restaurants.” Good Truckin’ REO Bites in REO Town. Photo by Lieza Klemm/City Pulse Gorman runs Good Truckin’ REO Bites with business partner Nick Sinicropi. While getting the restaurant open took longer than expected, Gorman said the response from locals “has been amazing.” The set-up and menu are “completely different” from the diner in Old Town, Gorman said. Designed as a to-go eatery, menu items are mostly served in baskets with minimal silverware. “It’s a lot of handheld items,” Gorman said. As far as seating goes, inside the shop are four tabletops and three bar stools. Outdoor patio seating is also available. Offering a grab-and-go menu was not the original idea. According to Gorman, the plan was to open a pastry and ice cream shop. “Pastries are tough if they don’t sell,” she said. “You have to throw them away.” The owners pivoted and developed a new menu, still sticking close to the initial vision. “We had the sandwich and ice cream idea in our heads, and then we said, ‘Well, we probably shouldn’t only do sandwiches because it doesn’t leave a lot of room for people to have different options,” Gorman said. Good Truckin’ continues to impress in new Old Town digs So, naturally, they added tacos and hot dogs to the list. Customers can order a “pasketti” taco, which includes spaghetti, meatballs with marinara, topped with mozzarella cheese. The taco also has a vegan option. From the sandwich list, the “meatball hero” jumps out. The hoagie comes with meatballs, marinara and mozzarella. Like its taco sister, the sandwich can be veganized. Customers can also order a “low country” hot dog, topped with bacon jam, pimento cheese and candied jalapeño. Good Truckin’ reemerges in REO Town Inspiration for the inventive offerings comes from the very first menu the owners offered over a decade ago. “[It] was already kind of wacky to begin with,” Gorman said. “It’s just gotten more creative over the years.” “So now you can get a meatball taco.” Besides the notable creativity, the menu includes options for those with dietary restrictions. As it stands, the shop has vegan meatballs, bacon, turkey, cheese and hot dogs. Almost all of the sauces are vegan too. “We look around Lansing, and options are very limited,” Gorman said. She and business partner Sinicropi are both vegan. “We want to be inclusive to all diets and all price ranges as much as we can.” Other menu items include soft serve ice cream, cold brew, hot coffee, breakfast sandwiches and a rotating list of pastries. Good Truckin’ REO Bites is open from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday, and closed Sunday and Monday.

articles.title: New poll of Jewish voters signals fatigue
articles.description: A new survey of Jewish voters in Michigan is shedding some light on how the community approached this year’s general election.
articles.content: A collection of "I Voted" stickers at a Michigan polling precinct on Election Day on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.(Rob Hess / Michigan Public )The poll, commissioned by The Jewish Majority, got text message responses from 883 self-identified Michigan Jews between October 25 and November 10.In it, Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed underperformed Democratic Governor-elect Jocelyn by 18 percentage points. Those who voted against El-Sayed mostly named his criticism of Israel and his comments after an attack on a Michigan synagogue as their top reasons for not supporting him.“Both parties should be looking at the Jewish vote right now and seeing an electorate in flux," said Jonathan Schulman, The Jewish Majority's executive director. "Those are votes that are up for grabs and in this polarized environment in which we are currently operating, both sides should be looking to gain whatever advantage they can and courting the Jewish vote should absolutely be on the table,” Schulman said.Most surveyed Jews still supported El-Sayed’s campaign.Ahead of the election, the group Nonnegotiable collected signatures to get El-Sayed to soften his tone toward Israel. But another Jewish-led group, Michigan Jews for Democracy, declared their support for El-Sayed’s campaign with a petition of its own.In the new survey, around two-thirds of respondents identified as Democratic or Democratic-leaning. Two-thirds also felt a connection to Israel as part of their Jewish identity.Schulman said, as both Democrats and Republicans become more willing to distance themselves from supporting Israel, many Jews are feeling politically displaced.“I think that for most Jewish voters, the idea that either party represents them right now is becoming increasingly rare,” Schulman said.This was a banner year for Democrats as they took back Congress and won several state races across the country. But Schulman views that as an outlier, meaning he believes Jewish voters could tip elections in the future.

Detroiters protest $548M tax subsidy for RenCen redevelopment
articles.description: The Detroit City Council is preparing for a final vote on a $2.2 billion redevelopment of the Renaissance Center and East Riverfront that relies heavily on taxpayer subsidies. Some advocates are protesting the deal, saying it will divert money from Detroit neighborhoods.
articles.content:
A 3D conceptual site plan illustrating the proposed "East Riverfront Concept Plan."(Bedrock)A plan to reshape Detroit’s skyline and East Riverfront is heading to the Detroit City Council for a final vote after being cleared by the city's Planning and Economic Development Committee. The redevelopment project would demolish two towers of the Renaissance Center to make way for new housing and a riverfront park.The City of Detroit, Detroit Economic Growth Corporation, Bedrock and GM are planning on investing $2.2 billion dollars to the project that will occur in 3 phases and is projected to be completed by 2026. $548 million of that investment will be from tax subsidies.A map outlining the official "Impact Area" for the Renaissance Center and East Riverfront redevelopment.
(City of Detroit )For many residents and local advocacy groups, the allocation of public funds to private developers is a misuse of city wealth, even though developers are pledging to give a total of $133 million dollars back to the city in exchange for the tax subsidies.$43.5 million of the money will go towards actual cash spent on community programs, affordable housing, and neighborhood initiatives:$15M in housing for neighborhoods outside of downtown and towards the city's trust fund that supports affordable housing. $10M towards small businesses and to provide business relief.$8M to fund a community hub including $1.5 million for youth programs.$6M towards job training programs for skilled trades and STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, Mathematics) careers.$4.5M for resident parking that'll allow Detroit residents to park for free for 1.5 hours at the site.Theo Pride, an organizer with the Detroit People’s Platform, condemned the proposed subsidy as "corporate welfare" and a "land grab" by the state's wealthiest interests."That's a half a billion dollars of our public wealth that should be going to our babies, that should be going to our seniors," Pride said. "Yet it's going to someone worth more, actually double than the yearly income of every single Detroiter combined."Pride emphasized that this massive financial commitment ignores the realities of Detroit's neighborhoods such as gentrification. He says that over 100,000 Black residents have been pushed out of the city over the last decade.He argued that working-class Detroiters are continually asked to pay the heavy price of displacement for downtown progress while seeing little return on public investments."Give them the land, give them the public money, they'll build some stuff and create a couple of construction jobs," Pride said, imitating past rhetoric. "But we don't get the housing, we don't get the jobs. All we do is get pushed out and displaced."Pride also demanded a structural change."We don't need an amusement park on the riverfront to be managed by some C4 nonprofit. What we need is public ownership in this deal," he stated. "We will not be made invisible in the city that we love, no matter how Bedrock wants to see Detroit and no matter how indecent they say we are".The Detroit City Council is expected to cast the deciding vote this month.

articles.title: Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday
articles.description: One way or another, the company will get some more data on Saturday.
articles.content: STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years. The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase. The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit.Read full article Comments

He continued, “No one from Skydance has even seen the movie – the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. Michigan’s Arab American News publisher sues Mike Rogers, campaign over alleged defamation
articles.description: Comments made by Republican former U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers and members of his campaign during the 2026 cycle are the focus of a defamation lawsuit filed by Osama Siblani, the editor of the Michigan-based Arab American News. The lawsuit, filed Thursday in Wayne County Circuit Court, alleges that Rogers and his campaign published and […]
articles.content: Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers, takes a question from moderator and political reporter Rick Albin, during a televised debate with Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed, at WOOD-TV, on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)Comments made by Republican former U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers and members of his campaign during the 2026 cycle are the focus of a defamation lawsuit filed by Osama Siblani, the editor of the Michigan-based Arab American News. The lawsuit, filed Thursday in Wayne County Circuit Court, alleges that Rogers and his campaign published and disseminated false statements of fact about Siblani. The lawsuit claimed that Rogers’ campaign had falsely stated that Siblani had called on American Jews to “return to Poland,” that he justified the Hamas terrorist attacks against Israeli citizens on Oct. 7, 2023, and had defended acts of terrorism more broadly. Siblani’s attorneys also allege that the Rogers campaign suggested he had a “group” that provided hundreds of thousands of dollars to El-Sayed’s campaign. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Rogers and his campaign were heavily criticized during the general election cycle for using Islamophobic rhetoric in its battle for the U.S. Senate seat against El-Sayed. Rogers also platformed several right-wing influencers and journalists who had produced stories claiming El-Sayed and his family had ties to terrorist networks or sympathizers, including the Muslim Brotherhood. Three members of Rogers’ campaign team were asked to comment on this story and the lawsuit. None responded at the time of publication. A statement from Rogers’ campaign will be added to this story when it becomes available. Aside from Rogers and his campaign, the lawsuit also names Together for Michigan, a group created to raise money and operate as “Democrats for Mike Rogers,” and outgoing state Rep. Karen Whitsett of Detroit. Whitsett was a member of the Democratic Party but left due to differences with her caucus. She became one of Rogers’ chief ex-Democrat surrogates on the campaign trail and helped run Together for Michigan and Democrats for Mike Rogers. Whitsett hung up on a Michigan Advance reporter twice while seeking comment for this story by phone. A text message seeking comment from Whitsett went unanswered by publication. A comment or statement from Whitsett will be added to this story when one becomes available. Michigan Rep. Karen Whitsett (D-Detroit) speaks alongside U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers at a “Democrats for Rogers” event in Detroit, Mich on Aug. 20, 2026 (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) Christine Fort, counsel for Together for Michigan, told the Advance that the organization has not yet seen a copy of the complaint. Fort did, however, provide a response to a retraction demand sent by Siblani’s attorney, James Allen, on Nov. 2. Fort said the response letter “addresses all of Siblani’s baseless claims.” “TFM declines to issue the requested retractions because the statements made in the advertisement were not defamatory — they were true,” Fort wrote. “‘[S]ubstantial truth is an absolute defense to a defamation claim.’ Alternatively, even if that were not the case, Mr. Siblani cannot come close to establishing that the statements in question were made with actual malice, which — as a public figure — he must prove for any defamation claim to lie.” Under a standard established by the U.S. Supreme Court, public figures must show that a defamatory statement was published either with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard for whether it was true. According to the complaint, the controversy stemmed in part from a Washington Free Beacon article that Rogers shared on social media. The article described Siblani as, among other things, “an unapologetic supporter of Hamas and Hezbollah.” The Free Beacon was not named as a defendant in the lawsuit but is referenced in the complaint. Free Beacon Editor-in-Chief Eliana Johnson told the Advance in an email that the publication stands by its reporting. “Siblani told Jewish Americans they should go back to Poland. Abdul said he was honored to have Siblani’s endorsement,” Rogers wrote in a post on X dated Oct. 27. “Abdul should disavow his endorsement and be held accountable for this hateful rhetoric that he champions. There’s no place for this in Michigan.” Siblani told Jewish Americans they should go back to Poland. Abdul said he was honored to have Siblani’s endorsement. Abdul should disavow his endorsement and be held accountable for this hateful rhetoric that he champions. There’s no place for this in Michigan. https://t.co/4yBv3cDsjl — Mike Rogers (@MikeRogersForMI) October 27, 2026 Siblani’s comments about Poland came at a 2024 rally in which he said “And to Netanyahu who wants to bring their people to the north, we are going to take you back to Poland.” It was made following Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s statement concerning the safe return of displaced Israeli residents to northern Israel. The phrase ‘Go back to Poland’ has been characterized as antisemitic because it invokes the trope that Jews have no ancestral ties to Israel. CNN’s Jake Tapper made that argument when discussing Siblani’s remarks in October 2024. Siblani’s lawsuit argues the comment was directed solely at Netanyahu, whose father was born in Poland. “Siblani did not demand that Jewish Americans return to Poland. His statement concerned only one individual, accused war criminal and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu specifically,” the lawsuit states. Some of Together for Michigan’s advertising for Rogers, which included TV spots and social media posts, was also a point of contention for Siblani. An Oct. 29 advertisement specifically named Siblani and called him a “notorious antisemite.” The ad also repeats the comments Siblani made at the 2024 rally. The “big tent” that includes notorious antisemite Osama Siblani, who wants to send Jews back to Poland? No thanks, Neera. There’s no room in the Democratic tent for virulent antisemites who sound indistinguishable from KKK members. https://t.co/luy4ODPc8P — Democrats For Mike Rogers (@DemsForMike) October 29, 2026 James Allen, Siblani’s attorney, wrote in the complaint that the allegations made against his client were “not merely unflattering descriptions, political opinions, or protected expressions of disagreement.” “They include purported statements of historical fact, attributed quotations, descriptions of specific conduct, and representations concerning objectively verifiable financial transactions that, if true, would violate campaign finance laws,” Allen wrote. “Defendants’ publications transformed these alleged statements and transactions into a narrative portraying Siblani as a defender of terrorists, an individual hostile to Jewish Americans as a group, and a substantial financial patron of El-Sayed — all of these allegations being demonstrably false.” The complaint states that Siblani acknowledges the First Amendment protects “robust political criticism” even if it is offensive or unfair. But his attorney argued that the U.S. Constitution “does not immunize the knowing publication of false statements of fact merely because they are deployed in a political campaign.” In her response to Sibani’s request for a retraction, Fort said “his personal distaste for the content of the communication or the manner in which he was portrayed is irrelevant, and does nothing to undermine the truthfulness of its claims.” “As stated above, the advertisement made no affirmative representations regarding Mr. Siblani’s sentiment toward Jewish Americans; rather, it simply allowed Mr. Siblani’s words to speak for themselves, accompanying them with an on-screen caption,” Fort wrote. “Having now demonstrated that the allegations and arguments you’ve presented herein fail to meet the minimum requirements of a defamation claim, let alone satisfy the actual malice standard that applies here, we will consider this matter closed.”

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services wrote […]
articles.content: Economic assistance application for the South Dakota Department of Social Services. (Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)WASHINGTON — The Trump administration announced Friday that states can take an additional six months to implement a provision in Republicans’ “big, beautiful” law that requires most people enrolled in Medicaid work, participate in community service, or attend an education program at least 80 hours a month. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services wrote in a statement that it’s established an “optional hold harmless period” to give state governments more time to update their systems and improve the processes they have in place. “States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries—at scale and for the long term,” Director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services Dan Brillman wrote in the statement. “If the state can use data to show that someone is working or qualifies for an exclusion, that person should not have to track down paperwork to prove it. And when someone needs support, they should know exactly what to do, when to do it, and where to go. That’s how we build a Medicaid program that works better for people, connects them to work, education, and training opportunities, and supports paths to prosperity.” Democrats in Congress raised concerns as recently as this week that states hadn’t had enough time to prepare for the new 80-hours-a-month requirement. House Energy and Commerce Committee ranking member Frank Pallone Jr., of New Jersey, and Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden, of Oregon, wrote in a letter dated Wednesday that administration officials use their “discretion to give states additional time to implement work reporting requirements and protect eligible beneficiaries from losing coverage.” The provision in the law requires Medicaid enrollees between the ages of 19 and 65 to work, participate in community service, or attend an education program for at least 80 hours a month. The law detailed several exceptions, including for pregnant people, parents of dependent children, people who have complex medical conditions, tribal community members, those in the foster care system, people who were in foster care who are below the age of 26 and individuals released from incarceration in the last 90 days, among others.

State Senator-elect Abbas Alawieh on priorities for Michigan's 2nd district
articles.description: State Senator-elect Abbas Alawieh spoke about the responsibility he feels as an Muslim and Arab American in a position of political power, and the issues he'll be prioritizing as the legislative session begins.
articles.content: State Senator-elect Abbas Alawieh speaks with April Baer in the Stateside studio.( Michigan Public)State Senator-elect Abbas Alawieh defeated Republican candidate Harry Sawicki in the race for Michigan's 2nd district, which includes Dearborn, Dearborn Heights, Allen Park, Melvindale, and Taylor. Alawieh made history as the state's first Muslim and Arab-American senator. "...I'm not running to be an Arab and Muslim American leader," Alawieh said. "I'm running to be a leader of every single person in the 260,000-person district that I represent. And I just want this part of my identity to just be a part of my story. Not all of it." Alawieh was a co-founder of the Uncommitted movement, and is an outspoken advocate against Israel's war on Gaza. He previously worked as congressional Chief of Staff to Rep. Cori Bush, and as a legislative staffer for Rep. Rashida Tlaib and Rep. Andy Levin. Alawieh acknowledged his constituents' concerns about affordability, as well as general concerns about protecting democracy."When I would knock on people's doors... they're worried about a federal government that is slowly chipping away at the very foundations of our democracy," Alawieh said. "And so I've spoken with governor-elect Jocelyn Benson, about her desire to see a Michigan Voting Rights Act on her desk and signed within those first 100 days, and I intend to be one of the leaders who helps deliver that."Alawieh spoke with April Baer about the responsibility he feels as an Muslim and Arab American in a position of political power, and the issues he'll be prioritizing as the legislative session begins.Scroll up to listen to the full interview, or read the transcript below:April Baer: This is an incredible year for a lot of Arab American and Muslim voters. Are you the first state senator who's Arab and Muslim?Abbas Alawieh: Arab and Muslim American, I believe. So we've got, I think, at least several folks who have had Arab Ancestry in the state legislature. But as far as I'm aware, you know, that is one historic first.AB: Congratulations.AA: Thank you so much.AB: Your district is a Democratic stronghold, so your real race was the primary. What went through your mind on primary election night when it became clear that you were going to win?AA: Primary election night was very emotional for us, both because, I'm just someone who's going to do the work all the way through the finish line. And so even though we ended up winning by 18 points, if you would have asked me [during the] primary election, I said, "It's very close. It's very close." And before the general, you know, where Democrats have won up and down the ballot, if you would have asked me, [I would have said,] "It's very close. We've got to run through the finish line." And so at first, it was actually quite unbelievable. But, I don't know if you know this, but it ended up being that right as we were getting the results, and I was excited to go out and announce that we had won and gave a victory speech, in that moment, we got notice that my grandfather, who lives in East Dearborn, had just passed unexpectedly. And so I went from being at my election night watch party, where we were about to make history, to being in his living room with him having just passed. And with my close cousins doing the things that a family has to do when a loved one passes. And so, I had seen him earlier in that day, and he prayed for our success. And we had so many polling locations covered. And it was all his kids, you know, my aunts and uncles, my mom, his nieces and nephews, his grandkids. And so his own influence and thumbprints were all over our primary win. And that's really special, because so much of the message of our campaign from the outset was, "We're running, and I'm running to take care of every single person in Senate District 2like I care for my own family." And so that family thread, I think was both important for me personally, certainly was important for me that night. But it's also important for a district that has undergone a lot of political turmoil, I would say, over the last few years especially.AB: I'm really sorry for your family's loss.AA: Thank you.AB: Your grandfather didn't live to see you make that victory speech that night, but he certainly saw you deeply involved in all kinds of community, from your work as a congressional staffer, to your work in the 2024 presidential race, and everything that that came after that. But there's also, you know, especially in 2024 when I would be on national TV advocating for a ceasefire, advocating for a stop to the endless flow of weapons to fund endless war. I'm Senator-elect now. I'll be sworn in in January. And already the deluge — I mean, certainly I experienced it in the primary, and certainly since the general — but there's a certain level of hostility that you endure as a Muslim American in public life. We saw that with Senator elect Abdul El-Sayed's campaign and experience. And that's not easy. Here I am running for office two years later. Jack Lang, of course, has been pardoned by Donald Trump. And every time that he came to town during the primary election season, actually two different times, my office was attacked. My campaign office was attacked in acts of racial intimidation, or ethnic intimidation. At one point, at one time, there was a brick thrown at my name that was outside. And it was scary. AB: Just to be clear, do you attribute that to him and his team? Or to the emotions of the time when people who follow him were encouraged?AA: The latter. I don't think it was him and his team, but certainly the level of hate that he was inviting into our communities here. So I went from, you know, understanding what he and people like him were trying to do to our democracy in Washington, D.C. And now, here I am, back in my campaign office in Dearborn and Dearborn Heights, and people are inspired by his hateful rhetoric, by his Islamophobic rhetoric, to attack my office. And for me, what it clarifies for me is that the likes of Jake Lang and other folks who are animated by the Islamophobic rhetoric that we're seeing from the president on down — they're not they're not attacking just Muslims, right? And I know, as evidenced by their involvement in January 6th, their contempt is for our democracy itself. It's for a democracy that can include everyone, including Muslim Americans. And that's why I think it's really important for us to fight as hard as we can for this, for democracy.AB: Now that you're an elected official yourself at the state level, can you talk to us a little bit about how you intend to put the priorities you expressed on the campaign trail, including maybe some of those health issues, into practice? This is a time when a lot of self-employed Michiganders have seen their premiums go through the roof, and we're looking at some huge cuts to Medicaid, which, of course have been passed along from the federal government. What's your first hundred days looking like?AA: Well, we've got to walk and chew gum at the same time on some of these issues. It's going to require us fighting for policy change while also doing that downstream work of "visiblizing" our constituent services operations to help as many people as possible hold on to the care that they need. So many people now, as a result of the failed policies and the really cruel policies that we're seeing handed down from the federal government, are about to be kicked off of Medicaid, or subjected to work requirements and reporting requirements that are so cumbersome, so hard to keep track of, especially for working people who are just trying to make ends meet. articles.content: The Federal Administration lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop after several hours Friday evening. Domestic flights were cleared to begin taking off at 8:35 pm EST. articles.title: FAA grounds all US flights due to air traffic control issue
articles.description: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for all flights in the United States on Friday due to communication problems. Air space opened up again at about 8:15 p.m. Eastern, officials said in in a White House briefing Friday night. In a statement, the FAA said all flights were grounded “due to extraordinary […]
articles.content: Travelers move through Salt City Lake International Airport in Salt Lake City on Oct. 16, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch)The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for all flights in the United States on Friday due to communication problems. Air space opened up again at about 8:15 p.m. Eastern, officials said in in a White House briefing Friday night. In a statement, the FAA said all flights were grounded “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in an X post that a communications problem was affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centers. The stop is the most severe shutdown of air travel since the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in 2001, according to reporting from The New York Times. “We have no reason to believe as of right now that this was a threat to the United States,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at the White House on Friday afternoon. “This was a telecommunication outage throughout FAA. Now, out of abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights, and all the flights are accounted for.” Mullin also said there was no indication the issue was connected to the widespread Microsoft outage earlier this week. U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, an Illinois Democrat who serves as ranking member on the Aviation Subcommittee, said that the ground stop “will warrant a thorough and complete investigation.” While the cause of the issue is not yet known, some have noted that the FAA recently expanded the use of an artificial intelligence tool to assist in managing air traffic. The agency has said the tool only suggests routes and will not affect safety, but some Democrats have raised concerns about its rollout, Gizmodo reported. When asked about the possibility that the issue could be related to AI, Mullin said “you just can’t rule out anything at this point.” “This is unprecedented when you see something like this,” Mullin said. “It’s going to take some time, and so this isn’t going to just be resolved and turned around within the hour.”

articles.title: TWTS: Sort of out of sorts
articles.description: When we are out of sorts, we’re not out of something specific, like socks or letters, but we may be feeling owly.
articles.content: Feeling out of sorts is something most of us experience from time to time. Maybe we're a little irritable, a little sad, or just not quite ourselves. But if we're out of sorts, does that mean we can also be in sorts?The Oxford English Dictionary dates the expression "out of sorts" back to at least 1621, though "sort" itself has been around much longer. It appeared in English in the late 1300s, referring to a kind, species, or variety of people or things. It could also refer to someone's character or rank.There was an earlier meaning of "sort" that was connected to the Latin word for "fate" or "fortune." That meaning eventually fell out of use during the Renaissance, around the same time "out of sorts" began appearing. It's not entirely clear whether the expression originally suggested a lack of quality or a lack of good fortune.Today, being "out of sorts" generally means we're not in our usual good spirits. It can mean feeling irritable or peevish, or simply feeling a little off. The expression has been relatively popular since the late 1800s, with a resurgence over the past couple of decades. We're particularly likely to say we're "feeling" out of sorts, or that we're "a little" out of sorts.While there's no real equivalent of being "in sorts," there are a few other expressions built around "sort." The phrase "in a sort" once meant "in a particular way," while "of sorts" can suggest something that's only approximately what it's supposed to be, such as "a celebration of sorts."The next time you're feeling out of sorts, you might try saying that you're feeling "owly." Professor Anne Curzan heard about this Canadian/Midwestern U.S. expression while listening to the podcast A Way With Words. For more on "owly" and some of the other ways we use "sort," listen to the audio above.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
articles.description: Nvidia poured tens of billions into AI startups under Huang. Without him at the helm, founders and VCs are bracing for smaller checks and lower valuations.
articles.content: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term. Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. “She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.” Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said. For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal. “Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.” It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position. If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.) Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang. Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs. While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did. Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations. Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations. “When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking. Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom. Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Marina Temkin is a venture capital and startups reporter at TechCrunch. Prior to joining TechCrunch, she wrote about VC for PitchBook and Venture Capital Journal. Earlier in her career, Marina was a financial analyst and earned a CFA charterholder designation. Report: Half of Michiganders with disabilities struggle to afford basic costs
articles.description: The United Way released an analysis that estimated in 2024 there were about 694,000 Michiganders with disabilities who fell below the ALICE threshold, which aims to calculate the cost of living.
articles.content: This story also appeared in Bridge Michigan The United Way released an updated estimate on the number of Michiganders with disabilities who fall below its ALICE threshold The threshold indicates the number of people living above the federal poverty level but who still struggle to pay for basic needs In 2024, about 29% of Michiganders with disabilities fell under the ALICE threshold, according to the estimate About half of Michiganders with disabilities struggle to afford the cost of living, according to newly released data from the United Way. The group estimates that in 2024, about 1.4 million Michiganders, or 14% of the population, had at least one disability, which included ambulatory, cognitive, hearing or vision disabilities. Of that group, about 20% fell below the federal poverty level. But another 29% were living above the poverty level, but still struggling to afford basic needs, a category that the United Way calls ALICE, or Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed. The United Way’s ALICE analysis attempts to estimate the number of people and households that don’t meet the federal government’s definition of poor, but don’t earn enough to afford basic housing, child care, food, transportation, health care or technology needs. The United Way says it uses its ALICE analysis to “illustrate the pervasiveness of financial hardship in the United States.” It sees ALICE as an alternative to the federal poverty level, which in 2026 was $15,960 for an individual and $33,000 for a family of four. All told, the United Way estimated that in 2024 there were 694,185 Michiganders with disabilities, or 49%, who were struggling financially. It was an estimated 48% in 2019. Across the country, about 18% of people with a disability fell below the federal poverty line and an additional 32% under the ALICE limit. “People with disabilities are our neighbors, friends and family. They’re woven into the fabric of our communities,” Kaitlynn Lamie, president and CEO of the Michigan Association of United Ways, said in a news release. “Yet too many face a system that makes basics like healthy food, transportation, and accessible housing and child care harder to obtain. The ALICE data helps us identify where gaps exist, so that we can direct our response where it’s needed most.” Related: Parents of Michigan students with disabilities demand special education reforms 5 Michigan cities voted to create ‘health action’ boards. Now what? Report: Funding, opportunity gaps hurting educational progress in Michigan There isn’t universal agreement on the ALICE threshold. In 2024, the Mackinac Center for Public Policy criticized the United Way’s methodology for the analysis, saying its definition of households under the threshold is “simplistic” and guarantees large groups of people fall under its level. US Census Bureau data released in 2024 estimated that about 13.2% of Michiganders and 12.5% of Americans were below the poverty level. Matt Mencarini is a Report for America corps member who covers data and accountability for Bridge Michigan.

articles.title: Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed
articles.description: Cost and access barriers are pushing people to modified use and unapproved versions.
articles.content: GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy. In a study published this week, researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That's around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Proposed UP conservation project would protect more than 150,000 acres while allowing commercial logging
articles.description: The agreement would prevent development, preserve wildlife habitat and guarantee public recreational access while commercial timber harvesting still continues. The post Proposed UP conservation project would protect more than 150,000 acres while allowing commercial logging appeared first on WDET 101.9 FM.
articles.content: The agreement would prevent development, preserve wildlife habitat and guarantee public recreational access while commercial timber harvesting still continues. Wetlands where birds of prey, such as Bald Eagles, make their home. The Great Lakes Forest Basin conservation project spans portions of the Lake Superior and Lake Michigan watersheds in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. The basin region includes 231 miles of rivers and streams, 11,500 acres of wetlands and more than 20,400 acres of critical deer wintering habitat. Under the proposal, Lyme Great Lakes Timberlands would retain ownership of the property, while the Department of Natural Resources would hold conservation easement rights on behalf of Michigan residents. The agreement would prevent future development, protect wildlife habitat and guarantee permanent public access. During a recent public tour of the property, representatives from the DNR and Lyme Great Lakes Timberlands demonstrated how modern forestry practices allow commercial timber harvesting to continue while protecting natural resources. The proposed conservation easement would protect habitat for numerous wildlife species, including deer, wood turtles, black bears, wolves, pine martens, fishers and bald eagles. Karen Sexton, a field manager with the DNR Wildlife Division, said deer wintering areas and wood turtle habitat are among the project’s major conservation priorities. “Beyond that, there’s…a variety of wildlife that’s going to benefit. [A lot of] the practices are already benefiting wildlife. Whether it’s early successional forest regenerating… to preserving some of the riparian areas (ecosystem areas where land meets the water) along watersheds,” Sexton says. “(It) also provides great corridors for wildlife to move through as well.” Unlike land purchased outright for public ownership, a working forest conservation easement allows private owners to continue commercial timber production while permanently restricting other land uses. Nathan Christie is with Lyme Great Lakes Timberlands. He says the agreement would prevent the forestland from being converted into residential developments, agricultural operations, among other potential uses. “Like if we were to sell some of these parcels, which we could, and future companies could, if it wasn’t in the CE (conservation easement), it could turn into a camp. It could turn into a farm. It could turn into a solar field. Stuff like that. This is forested now, forever,” he says. The project is possible through the federal Forest Legacy Program, which supports the conservation of environmentally important privately owned forestlands. For Michigan residents, the agreement would also preserve public natural recreational access to a vast area of Upper Peninsula forestland for future generations.

articles.title: US Supreme Court to decide on Trump ban on asylum claims at the border
articles.description: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court Friday granted the Trump administration’s request to decide whether the federal government can ban asylum claims at the southern border. One of President Donald Trump’s first proclamations he signed at the start of his second term was a ban on asylum claims at the southern border on the grounds […]
articles.content: A section of the U.S.-Mexico border wall near El Paso, Texas, on June 6, 2024. (Photo by Ariana Figueroa/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court Friday granted the Trump administration’s request to decide whether the federal government can ban asylum claims at the southern border. One of President Donald Trump’s first proclamations he signed at the start of his second term was a ban on asylum claims at the southern border on the grounds that there was an “invasion,” which the administration argued was a condition that allowed the president to invoke a section of the law to suspend asylum claims. A federal judge found the policy unlawful, but decided to allow it to remain while litigation pursued. An appeals court upheld the lower court’s decision. The justices agreed to answer two questions, whether the proclamation that bans asylum is lawful and if a class action suit should be allowed. The case will be argued sometime during the coming months. This is the third major immigration-related case the high court has agreed to hear this term. The justices also will decide whether the Trump administration can deport immigrants to countries to which they have no ties to and whether immigrants can be indefinitely detained. The justices earlier this year allowed the Trump administration to use a policy known as “metering” which allows immigration officials to turn away migrants applying from asylum at the southern border. The American Civil Liberties Union is representing the three immigration groups that brought the suit: the Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, the Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center and the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project. “The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.” A decision from the justices is likely next summer.

articles.title: Extended legal protections for Afghans sought in US House discharge petition
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Colorado Democratic Rep. Jason Crow, a military veteran, is making an attempt during Congress’ lame-duck session to provide legal protections for Afghanistan immigrants who aided the U.S. military for years, but now face swift deportations. Earlier this week, Crow filed a discharge petition. If he gains 218 signatures, he can force a House […]
articles.content: U.S. Rep. Jason Crow, a Colorado Democrat, shown on Feb. 3, 2025, is trying during Congress’ lame-duck session to provide legal protections for Afghanistan immigrants who aided the U.S. military for years, but now face swift deportations. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)WASHINGTON — Colorado Democratic Rep. Jason Crow, a military veteran, is making an attempt during Congress’ lame-duck session to provide legal protections for Afghanistan immigrants who aided the U.S. military for years, but now face swift deportations. Earlier this week, Crow filed a discharge petition. If he gains 218 signatures, he can force a House vote on his measure, H.R. 9899, which would allow certain Afghan nationals to qualify for Temporary Protected Status until July 2029. So far, the discharge petition has 114 backers, with two Republicans, Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Don Bacon of Nebraska, on board. There are 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats and one independent in the House. “After more than two decades of war, we made a promise that we’d look after them. It’s both a moral and national security imperative that we keep that promise,” Crow said in a statement. “I’m working to force a vote that will protect Afghans already in the United States because I won’t let our nation leave these brave Afghans behind.” The Trump administration has moved to effectively end the TPS program that Congress created in the 1990s to temporarily grant relief for nationals hailing from countries deemed too unsafe for return. The administration also has sought to revoke humanitarian protections, including TPS, for Afghans initially given under the Biden administration. The Department of Homeland Security initially moved to deport hundreds of Afghan allies to Pakistan, where they would likely then be removed to Afghanistan, but paused those efforts, which Bloomberg Law first reported. The practice of removing a noncitizen to a country with which they have no ties and then back to a home country where they will face harm is known as refoulement and it’s prohibited under international law. The Taliban currently controls the government in Afghanistan and the State Department’s travel advisory for the country is at the highest level, which means it advises against traveling. DHS estimated that there were roughly 11,000 Afghan nationals with TPS before then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem revoked protections in May 2025. Legal protections sought Crow is a former paratrooper and Army Ranger who was deployed to Afghanistan and has long petitioned for thousands of Afghan allies to receive legal protections after the chaotic 2021 U.S. withdrawal from the country that resulted in the Taliban taking over. Many of those Afghan allies and their families had to flee because of likely harm from the Taliban, a terrorist organization, for aiding the United States. “Our Afghan partners put their lives on the line to help protect American servicemembers like me,” Crow said. While Crow’s discharge petition might reach the 218-vote threshold for a vote, it will likely not move in the Senate, which Republicans control, or reach the 60 votes needed to advance. But in the 120th Congress, Democrats and independents who caucus with them will have 55 votes in the Senate, potentially 56 if Democrat Mary Peltola wins the Alaska race against GOP incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan. Passing any legal protections for immigrants, especially nationals from Afghanistan, will likely face a veto from President Donald Trump, and need a two-thirds majority to override. During his second administration, Trump instituted a ban on nationals from Afghanistan, and directed the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to stop processing legal immigration paperwork for Afghans after last year’s National Guard shooting in Washington, D.C. A federal judge in June ordered the Trump administration to continue processing that paperwork. The person charged with killing West Virginia U.S. Army Spc. articles.description: The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
articles.content: DTW's McNamara terminal( Detroit Metro Airport (DTW))This is a developing story. Last updated Nov. 13, 2026 at 4:51p.m.WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon because of communications problems at regional air traffic control centers. The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said there is a communications issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers that direct planes en route between airports nationwide. He said FAA technicians are investigating. This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023 when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country.But much work remains. Duffy has said that another $30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it.___This story has been corrected to show the Sept. 11 attacks were in 2001.

Battle for US Senate majority leader sets off with Van Hollen uphill challenge to Schumer
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen has a considerable amount of support to shore up if he wants to become majority leader next Congress, a role New York Sen. Chuck Schumer appears far more likely to secure when votes are cast behind closed doors Dec. 1. Van Hollen, a senior member of the Appropriations […]
articles.content: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks as Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., looks on during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol on Feb. 2, 2023 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Drew Angerer/Getty Images)WASHINGTON — Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen has a considerable amount of support to shore up if he wants to become majority leader next Congress, a role New York Sen. Chuck Schumer appears far more likely to secure when votes are cast behind closed doors Dec. 1. Van Hollen, a senior member of the Appropriations Committee, said during a press conference in Denver on Friday “it’s important to give Senate Democrats a choice. “That’s what we just gave voters — all over the country — a choice,” he said. “They chose change, and I think that the Democratic caucus needs to be open to new ideas, a different way of governing and a different way of conducting and approaching politics.” Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland speaks at a rally in support of federal workers outside the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 19, 2025. (Ashley Murray/States Newsroom) Van Hollen also told reporters he will not run for the presidency in 2028. Earlier this year, the Maryland Democrat had said he was “kicking the tires” on a potential 2028 presidential bid. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, is far more likely to secure the votes needed to continue on in that rule, judging from statements as of Friday. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer speaks to reporters at the U.S. Capitol on June 17, 2025. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom) He wrote in a statement released shortly after Van Hollen announced his longshot challenge that he was “proud” of the number of seats Democrats flipped in this year’s midterm elections. “I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer wrote. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result – and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.” The comments indicate that Schumer has already locked in the votes needed to remain Democratic leader for the next two years. El-Sayed backs Van Hollen Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed told the Michigan Advance shortly before Van Hollen made his decision public that he planned to support his bid. “I was the first to be calling on him as the next leader, so I would love to see him run, and I’d love to see him as our next leader,” El-Sayed said. Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan posted her support for Van Hollen to social media, writing that he “is the leader and fighter we need to bring about real change, so no American is left behind.” “Minnesotans are demanding change,” she wrote. “Democrats need to deliver. That starts with new voices in our leadership.” Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin and Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders, who caucuses with Democrats, both indicated earlier this week they were open to voting for a challenger. Sanders said during a press conference he would not be voting for Schumer, but Slotkin said she would only vote for a candidate who had a clear plan for how Democrats should lead in the majority. “I think whoever wants to run this caucus should come forward with a plan on how they’re going to govern differently, what they’re going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people’s pockets and then in particular how they’re going to communicate differently,” Slotkin said, adding she did not intend to challenge Schumer. Maine Sen.-elect Troy Jackson told reporters on Nov. 6 that he didn’t intend to vote for Schumer during leadership elections, according to WGME. “I’ve already said, I told Senator Schumer I’m going to support somebody else, so that’s no different now,” Jackson said at the time. Schumer allies: Schatz, King, Baldwin But other Senate Democrats rallied to Schumer as speculation swirled around Van Hollen and after the Maryland lawmaker formally announced his challenge. Hawaii Sen. Brian Schatz, who is likely to become whip next year, wrote in a statement that voters in this year’s elections “sent a clear message: they want us to lower costs, end a needless war, and fight corruption. “Our caucus has the right to have a conversation about the path ahead, but we have no time to waste. We must move quickly to vote, unify, and get to work. I endorse Senator Schumer for leader and will be voting for him in the caucus election.” Maine independent Sen. Angus King, who caucuses with the Democrats, wrote in a statement that “Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible.” “Chuck has outlined an aggressive plan for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” King added. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” Wisconsin Sen. Tammy Baldwin also made a reference to baseball when announcing her support for Schumer. “The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management,” she wrote. “The same is true in the Senate. Under Leader Schumer, Democrats won at least 55 seats. He earned his position as Majority Leader next Congress, and together we’ll deliver for Wisconsin families.” More senators’ opinions Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly indicated earlier this week that he would support Schumer, saying in a brief hallway interview that “he’s worked really hard to get this majority.” Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said Tuesday in a brief interview that he didn’t intend to share his thinking on the leadership races with reporters, though he didn’t explicitly say he’d support Schumer. “All the discussions about caucus leadership I’m having with my colleagues,” he said. “I’m not trying to give messages through the press.” Kaine said the most important policy work in the next Congress will be ending the war in Iran, undoing the tariffs and rescinding the changes to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program that Republicans included in their “big, beautiful” law. When asked by States Newsroom whether he believed Schumer is capable of accomplishing those goals for Democrats, he responded, “We are capable of doing them as a caucus.” Rhode Island Sen. Jack Reed, when asked whether he would support Schumer or a potential challenger, first said “I’m going to wait to see what develops. But Chuck has done a great job.” He added a few seconds later he planned to support Schumer. Nevadans back Schumer Nevada Sens. Jacky Rosen and Catherine Cortez Masto both threw their support behind Schumer in social media posts Thursday night. Rosen wrote Schumer “did the work to deliver what will soon be a 56-seat Senate majority against all odds, and I know he has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment.” Cortez Masto wrote Schumer “was instrumental in Democrats flipping 8 – soon to be 9 – Senate seats and securing a historic majority.”

articles.title: Report: Half of Michiganders with disabilities struggle to afford basic costs
articles.description: The United Way released an analysis that estimated in 2024 there were about 694,000 Michiganders with disabilities who fell below the ALICE threshold, which aims to calculate the cost of living.
articles.content: The United Way released an updated estimate on the number of Michiganders with disabilities who fall below its ALICE threshold The threshold indicates the number of people living above the federal poverty level but who still struggle to pay for basic needs In 2024, about 29% of Michiganders with disabilities fell under the ALICE threshold, according to the estimate About half of Michiganders with disabilities struggle to afford the cost of living, according to newly released data from the United Way. The group estimates that in 2024, about 1.4 million Michiganders, or 14% of the population, had at least one disability, which included ambulatory, cognitive, hearing or vision disabilities. Of that group, about 20% fell below the federal poverty level. But another 29% were living above the poverty level, but still struggling to afford basic needs, a category that the United Way calls ALICE, or Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed. The United Way’s ALICE analysis attempts to estimate the number of people and households that don’t meet the federal government’s definition of poor, but don’t earn enough to afford basic housing, child care, food, transportation, health care or technology needs. The United Way says it uses its ALICE analysis to “illustrate the pervasiveness of financial hardship in the United States.” It sees ALICE as an alternative to the federal poverty level, which in 2026 was $15,960 for an individual and $33,000 for a family of four. All told, the United Way estimated that in 2024 there were 694,185 Michiganders with disabilities, or 49%, who were struggling financially. It was an estimated 48% in 2019. Across the country, about 18% of people with a disability fell below the federal poverty line and an additional 32% under the ALICE limit. “People with disabilities are our neighbors, friends and family. They’re woven into the fabric of our communities,” Kaitlynn Lamie, president and CEO of the Michigan Association of United Ways, said in a news release. “Yet too many face a system that makes basics like healthy food, transportation, and accessible housing and child care harder to obtain. The ALICE data helps us identify where gaps exist, so that we can direct our response where it’s needed most.” Related: Parents of Michigan students with disabilities demand special education reforms 5 Michigan cities voted to create ‘health action’ boards. Now what? Report: Funding, opportunity gaps hurting educational progress in Michigan There isn’t universal agreement on the ALICE threshold. In 2024, the Mackinac Center for Public Policy criticized the United Way’s methodology for the analysis, saying its definition of households under the threshold is “simplistic” and guarantees large groups of people fall under its level.Donate US Census Bureau data released in 2024 estimated that about 13.2% of Michiganders and 12.5% of Americans were below the poverty level. Matt Mencarini is a Report for America corps member who covers data and accountability for Bridge Michigan.

articles.content: After launching its Dots AI agents platform earlier this year, OpenAI is launching a wallet for the agents. ChatGPT Wallet is rolling out starting today for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US aged 18 and older using a US billing address and “eligible US-issued American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa cards.” After adding a card to the wallet, your Dots agents can use it to buy things in response to your prompts, but they’ll check in with you each time before checking out. OpenAI’s support page says every purchase with ChatGPT Wallet requires a security check with biometric verification like Face ID or a fingerprint scan. [Image: Users have to approve every purchase from ChatGPT Wallet. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/openai-chatgpt-wallet-approval-pop-up.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Media: https://twitter.com/ChatGPT/status/2121283151729496235?a=Dzv0TkF6sRIc6NCqEso&s=20] After you review the AI agent’s purchase and sign off on it, OpenAI says that, similar to using tap to pay, Apple Pay, or Google Wallet, it substitutes your credit card details with a payment token, so your actual card info isn’t shared with your Dots agent or the business you’re buying from. Eventually, OpenAI says it expects “users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases.” ChatGPT Wallet might not work everywhere. Some retailers have restrictions on AI agents or block them altogether. Earlier this year, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agents. OpenAI says that in order for agents to use ChatGPT Wallet, “websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.”

articles.title: USDA delays grocery store rule after Mamdani appeal to Trump
Mamdani and Trump agree to delay on food stamp rules that put benefit at risk for millions
articles.content: New York City mayor says deal will allow bodegas and convenience stores across the country more time to comply Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, has struck a deal with Donald Trump to secure a 90-day delay on new rules for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap), so that bodegas and corner stores across the country have time to comply. The extension, Mamdani said, starts Friday as a result of conversations he had with Trump and Brooke Rollins, the agriculture secretary. The new guidelines, implemented by the US agriculture department, which retailers would have had to meet by 4 November, require stores to stock at least seven varieties within each staple food category: dairy, grains, protein and fruits or vegetables. Retailers would also have to ensure that they offer perishable items in three of the staple food categories. The new guidelines threw the lives of “more than a million New Yorkers” and “tens of milllions more across America” into “chaos”, the mayor said at a press conference on Friday. “People already reckoning with a shortage of affordable places to buy what they need for their home, soaring costs at the register, and food deserts across the five boroughs, now feared that the few places they could shop would no longer be able to accept their benefits,” Mamdani said. Several advocates were concerned that the new rules would mean people relying on Snap would be unable to buy groceries at their only accessible store. According to the Food Research and Action Center, bodegas, convenience stores and small grocery stores make up roughly 70% of Snap retailers. Given the tight timeframe to adjust their stock and meet the new requirements, small retailers ran the risk of going out of business if they couldn’t accept Snap benefits, the mayor said. “For so many of our fellow Americans, whether they shop at a general store in Michigan or a convenience store in Missouri, would have struggled to use their benefits and feed those they love.” More than 100 bodega owners reached out to Mamdani’s office with concerns about the new rule. According to the New York City department of city planning, there are more than 10,000 bodegas and corner stores across the five boroughs.
