articles.title: Fueled by Democratic gains, women will hold a record of state legislative seats
articles.description: The number of women serving in state legislatures will set a new record following strong Democratic performance in last week’s midterm elections. Though many races remain too close to call, an analysis by the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University shows at least 2,559 women will serve in state legislatures. That represents […]
articles.content: Members of the Colorado House of Representatives work on the floor during session in May 2022. Colorado has among the nation’s highest rates of women serving in the state legislature. (Pema Baldwin for Colorado Newsline)The number of women serving in state legislatures will set a new record following strong Democratic performance in last week’s midterm elections. Though many races remain too close to call, an analysis by the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University shows at least 2,559 women will serve in state legislatures. That represents nearly 35% of all state lawmakers and beats the 2026 record of 2,488 women in legislatures. Election results also show a new record of six state legislatures will reach gender parity, or at least 50% women: Arizona, California, Colorado, Delaware, Nevada and New Mexico, the center found. Those gains follow a historic election in which Democrats swept control of Congress, flipped hundreds of state legislative seats and won a majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years. Women will hold a record number of seats in state senates and state houses, though the rise is driven solely by the increasing number of Democratic women elected. In fact, the number of Republican women will fall in state legislatures next year — from 867 today to at least 675 in upcoming sessions. “While these are impressive gains for the overall number of women and Democratic women in state legislatures around the country, this is a significant decline for Republican women,” Debbie Walsh, director of the Center for American Women and Politics, said in a Friday news release. “…It is past time the Republican Party put in the work to mitigate the ever-widening partisan gap in women’s representation.” Current election results show women will hold about 35% of all state legislative seats next year. That figure is currently 32.43%, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. About 64% of the women currently in state legislatures are Democrats. Across the political spectrum, research shows lower levels of political ambition among women. Women tend to underestimate their own qualifications, are more averse to competition and receive less recruitment and encouragement to run for office. Many women also work full-time and are primary caregivers. But the number of women serving in legislatures has increased nearly 40% over the past decade, according to government relations firm MultiState. Still, representation varies wildly: Women hold more than half of seats in Colorado, Nevada and New Mexico, but fewer than 15% of seats in West Virginia, South Carolina and Mississippi. This election cycle also set a record for the number of women governors with at least 18 women slated to serve as their state’s executive. The midterms also notched other records: For the first time ever, five Black governors will serve simultaneously in the United States. Voters also elected the nation’s first Black woman governor, the first Black Republican governor and the first Native American woman governor. Congress will also see a record number of women serving. The center also tracked record numbers of Black, Latina and Native American women elected to Congress. Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org. This story was originally produced by Stateline, which is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network which includes Michigan Advance, and is supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.

articles.title: Beydoun faces 3 new charges in grant scandal, including alleged use of funds for her legal defense
articles.description: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced Friday afternoon three new charges against Fay Beydoun, the businesswoman who faces accusations of misusing $20 million in state legislative grant funding. The new charges allege that she used hundreds of thousands of dollars in funds from her nonprofit organization, which was funded with state grant money, for her […]
articles.content: The office of Attorney General Dana Nessel in the G. Mennen Williams Building in Lansing, Mich., on May 15, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced Friday afternoon three new charges against Fay Beydoun, the businesswoman who faces accusations of misusing $20 million in state legislative grant funding. The new charges allege that she used hundreds of thousands of dollars in funds from her nonprofit organization, which was funded with state grant money, for her own legal defense fund, as well as for a membership to a professional organization and for personal furniture purchases. Beydoun was charged in May with 16 felonies — conducting a criminal enterprise, forgery, larceny by conversion of more than $20,000, six counts of larceny by conversion involving $1,000 to $20,000 and seven counts of uttering and publishing. At that time, Nessel’s office said that the investigation was ongoing and could result in additional charges. Nessel’s press release detailed the background of the initial charges against Beydoun, which stem from a “Michigan enhancement grant” that she received through the fiscal year 2023 state budget to establish and operate a global business accelerator in Oakland County — her nonprofit, Global Link International (GLI). GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Now, Beydoun faces three additional charges related to the alleged theft of the funds, including two counts of larceny from a person, each a 10-year felony charge, “concerning an attempt to have GLI pay her legal expenses in defending herself against allegations that she stole from GLI, and for a donation to the Michigan Founders Fund alleged to be for personal reasons,” and one of larceny by conversion, a five-year felony. “These newly charged allegations reflect the continued investigative efforts ongoing in my office, and a broader extent of Beydoun’s alleged expenses made with state grant funding,” Nessel said in a press release announcing the new charges. She noted that the case — which had initially been scheduled for a preliminary examination in January but will be postponed because of the new charges — will stretch beyond her term, which ends at the end of 2026, and stated that the case “remains a top priority within our Financial Crimes Division.” When asked for comment by Michigan Advance, Beydoun’s attorney, Vincent J. Haisha, called the new charges “a stretch.” “In charging Ms. Beydoun with theft, the Department of Attorney General conveniently left out the fact that Global Link’s own board of directors approved these funds for legal fees. It labels as larceny a grant to the Michigan Founders Fund, a nonprofit that supports Michigan entrepreneurs, when not a dollar of that money went to Ms. Beydoun. And it treats as a crime Global Link’s purchase of office furniture, including a conference room table and reception-area pieces, at an estate sale for a fraction of retail,” Haisha said. “These charges don’t add strength to the Department of Attorney General’s case. They show how far it is reaching. Ms. Beydoun will answer them in court, where the facts will speak for themselves.” Beydoun’s grant, which was administered by the Michigan Economic Development Corporation (MEDC), was secured while she served on the MEDC Executive Committee, and Nessel’s office has alleged that “no business relocated to Michigan through Global Link International efforts. Instead, Beydoun is accused of using the funds for personal gain and maintaining a $550,000 annual salary.” “We allege Fay Beydoun sought and received a $20 million ‘Michigan enhancement grant’ from the state Legislature where she operated a criminal enterprise to use those funds for personal expenses and her own enrichment, and lied repeatedly when reporting how she used those funds, rather than using them towards the legally intended purpose of the grant,” Nessel said at the time of the initial charges. The initial charges against Beydoun led to calls for change in the structure and administration of the MEDC, which have continued as controversies around the agency continue. 4:58 pmThis story has been updated with comment from Beydoun's attorney.

articles.title: In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits
articles.description: In Sri Lanka, ecological change is shrinking a park's elephant population.
articles.content: Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time. Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured. Accidental savanna Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country's four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006).Read full article Comments

articles.content: The U.S. Capitol on the evening of Sept. 30, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — Dozens of incoming U.S. House Democrats are urging party leaders to tackle a stock trading ban for lawmakers on the first day of the 120th Congress in January. Just over 50 representatives-elect sent a letter Thursday to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Democratic Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and other top House Democrats asking that the House adopt a rule barring House members and their spouses from owning and trading individual stocks. “Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country. The existing laws around insider trading are insufficient. We should hold ourselves to the highest standard and work to restore faith in government. Nobody should leave Congress with millions more in their bank accounts,” according to the letter signed by 51 incoming House freshmen. More than half of the new members who signed the letter flipped their seats from Republican to Democrat. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them. This rule would be a down payment on much-needed reform to prevent elected and appointed government officials and their spouses from trading stocks. We promised our communities we would clean up this place. In January, we should do just that,” the one-page letter continued. Those who signed the letter include newly elected members in Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Iowa, Illinois, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, New Hampshire, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Wisconsin. The offices of Jeffries and Clark did not immediately respond to a request for a comment. A stock trading ban for members of Congress has gained bipartisan support over several years. Thirteen House Democrats joined all Republicans in passing a stock trading ban in July, though the bill received significant criticism from Democrats who said it did not go far enough, and because House Republicans attached the bill to a voter ID measure. Senate Democrats blocked the bill in September, solidly across party lines.

MSU Football Victory Sparked Over 50 Nuisance Fires, Strained Emergency Services
articles.description: Law enforcement officials are asking for the public to submit photos or videos that could help identify those responsible for the fires.
articles.content: The East Lansing Fire Department responded to 54 nuisance fires last weekend as Michigan State University football pulled off an upset victory in Ann Arbor over University of Michigan, local public safety leaders said during a news conference Friday. Ingham County’s 911 Central Dispatch saw a significant backlog as the East Lansing Fire Department, or ELFD, responded to 88 calls over a 24-hour window on the Saturday game day, ELFD Chief John Newman said during the news conference. “When fire crews and dispatchers are overwhelmed by dozens of preventable, intentionally set fires, every resident within our county is placed at risk if they experience a life-threatening emergency,” Newman said. The East Lansing Police Department has been collecting digital evidence, including social media photos and videos to identify the individuals involved with the decades-long tradition in East Lansing of MSU students setting couches on fire after athletic events, Newman said. Though no one has been charged in relation to the fires on Saturday yet, once detectives identify the parties involved, they will be held legally accountable and ELPD is asking for the public’s help in finding more images and videos from the fires. There’s likely going to be criminal charges coming out of the events of last weekend, Ingham County Sheriff Scott Wriggelsworth said during the news conference. As an MSU alum, he said there’s a lot to be proud of at MSU, but the couch fires are not a source of pride for the area. “I spent 20 plus years working for the East Lansing Police Department before being elected sheriff, and I’ve responded to hundreds … of these in my career, these nuisance fires associated with a win, a loss, or for some other reason, they’re not fun. They’re not funny. Frankly, they’re idiotic, and they’re super dangerous. They’re criminal offenses and should be treated as such,” Wriggelsworth said. A culture change is needed when it comes to MSU’s traditions, Wriggelsworth added, and MSU students who are found to be responsible for game-day fires should face disciplinary actions from the school. East Lansing public safety leaders are in conversations with the university in an effort to curb the fires, Newman said. East Lansing residents, which include students, are encouraged to report to law enforcement if they see individuals preparing to burn items. articles.content: MichMash speaks to State Rep. Ranjeev Puri (D), who was recently elected to be the next Speaker of the Michigan House. Puri discusses what worked for his party this election and what their priorities are now that they’ve won a majority. Democrats won a majority in Michigan’s senate and house this election, in addition to clinching the governor, secretary of state, and attorney general races. In the house, Michigan Democrats took 11 seats—the largest gain they’ve made since 1964. That makes the breakdown of Michigan’s house 63-47 next term. Gongwer News Service’s Zach Gorchow and WDET’s Cheyna Roth speak to State Rep. Ranjeev Puri, who was recently elected to be the next Speaker of the Michigan house. Puri discusses what worked for his party this election and what their priorities are now that they’ve won a majority. The midterm elections going in Democrat’s favor wasn’t “rocket science” says Speaker-elect Puri. “The policies that were coming out of DC, which kind of set the tone and narrative for this election cycle, were deeply unpopular. You didn’t see House Republicans or Michigan Republicans really ever stick up for team Michigan.” And on the other hand, he also attributes the party’s huge success on messaging that spoke to voters. “I think our campaigns spoke more acutely to making people’s lives in Michigan better…. We invested in 11 red-to-blue flip opportunities and we won all 11 of them.” Michigan’s legislature has been gridlocked for the past couple of years. Now that Democrats won big, they should have the momentum needed to make big changes come January. Among their priorities is passing the nine 2024 bills that Gov. Gretchen Whitmer vetoed earlier this year, as well as addressing health care costs, Canadian tariffs, utility costs and more. “Affordability was the talk of the cycle… [We need to ensure] that our health care access remains as strong as possible, especially with the ramifications of the Big Beautiful Bill being further exasperated as we start 2027,” says Puri. He’s looking forward to welcoming 26 new members to the state house and adding their perspectives to the experience of returning representatives. “The experience you get doesn’t only happen in majority,” says Puri. “I think there’s a lot of lessons that we’ve learned in our time in minority as well. I think it’s going to make us all better legislators.” One-of-a-kind podcasts from WDET bring you engaging conversations, news you need to know and stories you love to hear. Member States reiterate commitment to finalize Pandemic Agreement PABS Annex by May 2027
articles.content: Member States advanced negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) Annex to the WHO Pandemic Agreement, reaffirming their commitment to finalizing the Annex for its consideration by the World Health Assembly in May 2027. The PABS Annex would establish a system that ensures the rapid, transparent sharing of pathogens with pandemic potential and their genetic sequence data, while ensuring rapid and equitable access to the resulting products, including vaccines, diagnostics and therapeutics. The two-weeks long negotiations of the Intergovernmental Working Group (IGWG) on the WHO Pandemic Agreement reflected a strong determination among Member States to fulfill the mandate they set for themselves when adopting the Pandemic Agreement. “During the past two weeks, government negotiators have worked tirelessly and constructively to move the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing annex and agenda forward,” said Ambassador Tovar da Silva Nunes of Brazil, co-chair of the IGWG Bureau guiding the negotiations. “We have made important progress on both benefit-sharing and access provisions, while maintaining a shared focus on building a system that is practical, equitable and capable of delivering public health benefits when they are needed most.” Member states made progress on how to share benefits within a legally binding framework. Their discussions further clarified the roles of participating partners and explored how the PABS system can support more equitable access to pandemic-related health products when future threats emerge. Member States also advanced discussions on access to pathogens with pandemic potential, including the sharing of biological materials and sequence information, while undertaking detailed consideration of the role of laboratories and other technical partners in supporting the system. IGWG Bureau co-chair, Ambassador Anne-Claire Amprou of France, said: “The spirit of these discussions has been remarkably constructive. Through both formal and informal negotiations, Member States have demonstrated a strong commitment to finding common ground and refining the Annex so that we can meet the mandate entrusted to us and conclude our work by the next World Health Assembly in May 2027.” Throughout the negotiations, WHO experts continued to support Member States with scientific, legal and operational expertise that informed discussions and pushed for progress across complex issues. At the meeting’s closing, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghrebreyesus, recognized the progress of Member States in taking the PABS Annex negotiations forward, and reminded them of the importance of their work to help make the world safer from future pandemic threats. "I am reassured to hear the full commitment of delegations to conclude the negotiations in time for the World Health Assembly next year," said Dr Tedros. "What we need now is to translate that commitment into reality in the room, and to move decisively towards concluding the text. I have seen signs of that during IGWG9, and I hope you will carry that momentum forward.” Member States agreed to keep momentum in the coming months, including working to bring positions closer together through informal sessions. IGWG9 will resume formal negotiations during 11-15 January 2027. Additional rounds of formal negotiations are scheduled for 15-19 February 2027 and 15-25 March 2027. In May 2025, the World Health Assembly adopted the WHO Pandemic Agreement to strengthen international cooperation in preventing, preparing for and responding to pandemics. Member States also established an Intergovernmental Working Group to help advance the Agreement, including drafting and negotiating the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing Annex. Dedicated to the well-being of all people and guided by science, WHO leads and champions global efforts to give everyone, everywhere, an equal chance at a safe and healthy life. We are the United Nations’ agency for health that connects nations, partners and people in more than 150 locations – leading the world’s response to health emergencies, preventing disease, addressing the root causes of health issues and expanding access to medicines and health care. Our mission is to support all countries to promote, provide and protect health. “Together for health. Stand with science”, the theme of World Health Day 2026, marks a year-long campaign to highlight science as the foundation for protecting health and well-being worldwide.

articles.title: Election season's in full swing -- for 2028 that is.
articles.description: With the 2026 election season under wraps, Michigan is gearing up for its role in the 2028 presidential election cycle.
articles.content: (Kalloli Bhatt / Canva)Hi! You’re reading the It’s Just Politics newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the It's Just Politics podcast for all the political news you need each week.It’s been a little more than a week since the election. And politicians are doing what any politician would do: prepping for the next election cycle.Actually, the preparation, and Michigan’s role in it, started long before the 2026 Midterms, when the Democratic National Committee (DNC) approved Michigan to be the fifth state to hold a primary before Super Tuesday.Other early-primary states include South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, and New Mexico, with primaries before Michigan, and Virginia, with a primary after Michigan.This placement incites presidential hopefuls to start building relationships with Michiganders, elected officials, key unions, and other stakeholders well before announcing a campaign.Essentially, being fifth in the primary line adds power to Michigan's already important status as a swing state that could make (or break) a blue wall.And visit politicians did. The list includes, but isn’t limited to:California Governor Gavin Newsom, who campaigned with Senator-Elect Abdul El-Sayed in AugustFormer Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who stumped with Representative-Elect Sean McCann and Governor-Elect Jocelyn Benson New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who also campaigned with El-SayedIt’s important to remember that these political appearances were meant to support Michigan’s 2026 candidates, and don’t necessarily prove a desire for presidential candidacies. However, taken together, they show Michigan is already attracting attention from potential contenders.Habibi PACAdding to Michigan’s influence over the election in 2028, El-Sayed has formed a new leadership political action committee (PAC), named Habibi PAC.This type of PAC is unique in that it is specifically used to raise money for other candidates, for federal or nonfederal offices.As Michigan Public’s Zena Issa reported, political commentators view the launch of the PAC “as a classic strategic move to help El-Sayed build influence within the Democratic Party and position himself as a key player ahead of the 2028 presidential election cycle.”In other words, El-Sayed’s position as a Senator from a swing state has the potential to bring heightened attention to his political footprint and messaging. The leadership PAC allows him, through the candidates it supports, to put money around his campaign’s main talking points.But, that doesn’t mean people aren’t watching already. Neil Thanedar, executive director of the Michigan Campaign Finance Network (MCFN), pointed out to Issa that El-Sayed’s use of a PAC is a deviation from his stance on accepting PAC money during his campaign."It will be interesting to see who the donors are for this PAC and where the money goes, because Abdul El-Sayed has talked numerous times about not wanting to accept corporate PAC money and other special interest funding," Thanedar said.Taken together, El-Sayed’s new PAC and his relationships with nationally prominent Democrats could make him an influential figure beyond Michigan in the lead-up to 2028.Though, his success as a progressive candidate in a competitive state raises an interesting question for Democrats: Could his campaign offer a model for winning other battleground states in 2028?Only time will tell. But with Michigan positioned to vote early in the Democratic presidential primary, Michiganders won’t just have a say in who wins the White House, they’ll also have an early say in who gets a shot at it.And if the last election cycle is any indication, we’ll be seeing plenty more of the presidential hopefuls before then.ICYMI➡️Ohio Representative-Elect Don Leonard said, in a social video, that "senior Democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives threatened to make his time in Congress ‘a living hell’ if he doesn't support Hakeem Jeffries' bid to become U.S. Speaker of the House.” Read WOSU’s George Shillcock’s full story.What I’m watching: In reaction, social media influencers have begun encouraging Michigan’s freshman delegation to not support Jeffries. Essentially saying the people have your back, even if leadership doesn’t.➡️Bridge Michigan recently interviewed incoming Michigan House Speaker Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) on his priorities for his new position. He’ll replace outgoing House Speaker Matt Hall.What I’m watching: I'm curious if Puri will come up with an acronym that trumps the Hall Ethics, Accountability, and Transparency (HEAT) Plan.Until next time,Kalloli Bhatt, Digital Content Producer_______________________Have questions about Michigan politics? Or, just want to let us know what you want more of (less of?) in the newsletter? We always want to hear from you! Shoot us an email at politics@michiganpublic.org!____________________________________________________________________________________________

'His roots are here:' Muslim U-M students on what El-Sayed’s win means to them
articles.description: Students shared a visceral sense of pride after Abdul El-Sayed overcame a campaign riddled with Islamophobic claims and xenophobic tropes to become the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate.
articles.content: Muslimstudents (left to right) Hamza Said, Hadi Muhammad-Ali, Abdullah Ali, Aisha Siddiqui, and Mohid Rehman at Abdul El-Sayed's alma mater, the University of Michigan, felt moved by his electoral victory last week. El-Sayed will be the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate.(Rob Hess / Michigan Public)Growing up in Portage, Mich., Aisha Siddiqui said she was frequently in spaces where she couldn’t help but notice how different she was from others.“I was a very shy and nervous kid and already very insecure and just being the only girl of color, sometimes the only girl who had hijab on her head,” made her feel alienated, she said.That feeling was paired with a sense of being somehow responsible for everyone else who was like her. “As a Muslim,” Siddiqui, who is now a sophomore at the University of Michigan, explained, “You're expected to condemn and be able to carry the burdens of everything that every single Muslim has done at once.”It’s because of that vexxing double bind that she found Abdul El-Sayed’s historic win in last week’s election to be monumental: “[El-Sayed] brings that American-Muslim identity to the forefront and kind of shows that you can be both at once and you can be enough in both identities.”For many Muslims, seeing the physician and public health administrator become the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate feels like a moment for collective pride – especially following a campaign riddled with Islamophobic claims and xenophobic tropes.That sense of pride was visceral following Friday prayer in a side room of the student union at the University of Michigan – and perhaps only more so because El-Sayed served as the vice president of the Muslim Student Association.“His roots are here,” said Hamza Said, a junior. “He was in the same room praying with us. He was in the same room putting his shoes on and going out and going to classes.”Said felt especially moved by El-Sayed's visit to Friday prayers last year when he made a short speech and talked with students.“I've never really had any person in government that I could be like, ‘He's the same as me. He comes from the same place. He has the same values,’” Said said, who noted El-Sayed, like him, is Egyptian-American and studied pre-med. “I think one of the most inspirational people who I've ever met.”Many could also relate to some of the negative sentiments that trailed El-Sayed throughout his candidacy – including the repeated suggestion that his name somehow undermined his ability to serve in Congress.“I grew up in a majority white community where people had trouble pronouncing my name,” said Abdullah Ali, a senior studying astronomy. “So my name means a lot to me. It was a core piece in what helped me form my sense of self. And so all of the rhetoric surrounding [El-Sayed’s] name especially was very personal to me.”Ali added that he found the focus on El-Sayed’s name to be “bizarre,” adding that his opponents seemed keen to suggest his name meant he had some kind of “ulterior motives” to running for office.But Ali said he didn’t see the same kind of dismissive negativity when he talked to voters. He knocked on doors as a volunteer canvasser and said he had almost no negative interactions with people.“The few that I did have were almost entirely about his policy and never about his identity. And that was very touching to me – that real people like that don't carry that kind of hate in their hearts,” Ali said.For many Muslims, the immediate aftermath of 9/11 led to a sort of work hard and keep your head down ethos. But amidst increased surveillance and heightened scrutiny that followed, Muslims began to take a different tact – engaging in civic life and indeed, running for public office.El-Sayed is one of a growing number of Muslims elected to public office across the country.When he took the stage in Detroit on election night, El-Sayed began by saying his full name – Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed – and pronounced it as it’s meant to be said instead of the shortened, anglicized way he said it in political ads or campaign stops.That moment was full of meaning for many, including Aisha Siddiqui.“It just also goes to show that we don't always have to be digestible to the media and make ourselves smaller and confine ourselves to certain limits in space,” she said. “He can be Abdulrahman and still be our senator and still be an American and still provide for us the things that he promised us.”Michigan Public’s Rob Hess contributed to this story.

articles.description: For Abdul El-Sayed, winning the Nov. 3 election was never the ultimate goal — it was a good first step toward a seat at the table and a real chance to make change. Now that he’s U.S. Sen.-elect El-Sayed, he is not slowing down on his main policy goals. In an interview with Michigan Advance, […]
articles.content: WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 11: U.S. Senator-elect Dr. Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) poses for a photo in his office on the U.S. Capitol on November 11, 2026 in Washington, DC. El-Sayed defeated Republican Senate candidate, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-MI) in the midterm elections. (Photo by Salwan Georges/Getty Images)For Abdul El-Sayed, winning the Nov. 3 election was never the ultimate goal — it was a good first step toward a seat at the table and a real chance to make change. Now that he’s U.S. Sen.-elect El-Sayed, he is not slowing down on his main policy goals. In an interview with Michigan Advance, El-Sayed said he’s urging his colleagues in the incoming Democratic majority to strike while the moment is hot to make lasting change for the American people before their window of opportunity closes. Here’s what the senator-elect had to say about climbing “Mount Everest” to achieve his campaign promises and what’s next for the Democratic majority as it works to earn its mandate to govern. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Michigan Advance: Given the lay of the land in the U.S. House and U.S. Senate for the next session of Congress, what is your read on the potential for getting some of your chief campaign promises at least on the board next year? Does it look like Medicare for All is more possible than rolling back Citizens United? Abdul El-Sayed: I think there’s a lot of opportunity around a lot of these goals. Let’s focus on the affordability side. Ending the war, stopping dumb tariffs is a big goal for us, and that is going to put a lot more money back in people’s pockets. That’s a huge piece. The second, thinking about union protections, thinking about standing up to big corporate monopolies — all things I’d lived to do, that I’m looking at colleagues to be able to do. When it comes to Citizens United, I think there’s a lot of focus, given how expensive these midterms were, on addressing these challenges. I’ve already been talking to colleagues, frankly on both sides of the aisle, about how to do that. When it comes to expanding healthcare, the first thing we’ve got to do is make sure that they don’t cut more through these Medicaid cuts. From there, I think there’s a real opportunity to start getting expansions, if not all the way Medicare for All. Now, I’m really looking toward how we build momentum through 2028, so we elect a president who’s ready to do this and be ready on day one with the legislation. MA: You mentioned the potential for additional healthcare expansions first. How open are you to incremental changes as opposed to all-or-nothing changes? For example, if Medicare for All for kids is possible as a first step, would you support that, even though it doesn’t get everyone across the board? AES: I’ve been clear that I want to climb Mount Everest, and to climb Mount Everest, you’ve got to get to base camp. So, I understand that you’ve got to take multiple steps. It’s a long journey, but I’m not going to lose sight of the fact that we want to climb Mount Everest. It’s that kind of commitment that I think is critical. So yes, I’m going to take as much as I can get done within the space of where folks are willing to work, and then keep coming until we’ve gotten all the way there. U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, left, and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, right, at a rally with U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. House candidate William Lawrence in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance) MA: Looking to 2028, there’s going to be a big push for many, and I mean many, Democrats to seek the office of president. We’ve already seen signs that people are energetic, it seems, for someone like your colleague, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, to run. Which among the potential candidates that may be out there do you see as being in line with what you want to achieve in the U.S. Senate? Who would be best suited for this moment? AES: I’ve yet to see who’s actually running, so it’s a bit premature. I want somebody who’s ready to get money out of politics, put money in our pockets, and pass Medicare for All. I’m looking for somebody who understands Michigan and wants to serve our state and wants to be a governing partner to try and address the role that Citizen United has had in corrupting our politics; who wants to stand with unions, wants to take on corporate monopolies and oligopolies, and wants to guarantee everybody healthcare through Medicare for All. MA: As this new Democratic majority gears up to take over Congress next year, I think back to the early legislative trifecta of the Obama years. Looking back, Democrats wielded their power enough to get the Affordable Care Act, the American Recovery and Investment Act and Dodd-Frank signed into law, but then they lost the House in 2010. How important is it for you all to be as efficient, surgical and swift with your policy goals in this majority so you don’t lose the moment? AES: That’s exactly what we need to do. We cannot squander this governing opportunity that the public has given us, and we have to understand that it wasn’t as much a vote for us as it was a vote against them. So we have to earn our mandate by actually demonstrating action, and every single one of those actions has to be about addressing the affordability crisis in people’s lives. U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a rally in Ferndale, Mich., on July 25, 2026. U.S. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Van Hollen and U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal also spoke at the event. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance) MA: I know your primary opponent had framed her campaign as a “love letter to Michigan,” but on the campaign trail, you also showed Michigan a lot of love. An example: You had name-dropped a local shawarma shop that has seen a bunch of business since then. What does it mean to you, to know that there is a kind of excitement buzzing at a Michigan business simply because it was a place that you loved? AES: We have so many amazing small businesses in Michigan, and they deserve a spotlight. I hope that I can continue to shine spotlights on so many of them, because small business is the heart and soul of our economy. Folks have an idea and they turn that idea — through blood, sweat and tears — into a business and into a commitment to their local community. I hope that our fellow Michiganders will go and engage in the incredible work that they do every single day. There’s nothing better than folks coming together around a meal they love, or a design that they’re excited about, some flowers to bring to mom. It’s one of the best parts of the job. MA: Throughout the campaign, Republicans and others opposed to your candidacy made a lot of noise about your culture, your religion and your name. But your full real name — Abdulrahman — means “servant of the most Merciful” or “most Gracious” in Arabic. “The servant of God.” What does it mean for you, now as a member of Congress, to be in a position to serve a great many people, not just Michiganders, in the U.S. Senate? articles.title: Clinton Twp. police probe false weapons threat on school bus
articles.content: Clinton Township police responded to a false report of a weapon being on a school bus on Friday morning, police said. Authorities said a student attending Wyandot Middle in the Chippewa Valley Schools district overheard another student on the bus claiming they had a firearm in their possession. According to police, the school bus was in the vicinity of Cherokee Elementary School on Rivergate Drive at the time of the incident, initially causing confusion about which school the student involved attended. Officers made contact with the bus and student, and did not find any weapons, police said in a news release. Clinton Township police determined there was no active or ongoing threat to Cherokee Elementary School, Wyandot Middle School, or any surrounding Chippewa Valley Schools facilities. Friday’s incident was the second time this week police had a security incident involving Chippewa Valley Schools. On Tuesday, several CVS schools were placed in lockdown status after a swatting call to Dakota High School in Macomb Township forced school officials to take steps to protect students and employees. Three other nearby elementary schools — Seneca, Ojibwa and Cheyenne — were also placed in secure status, meaning no one could enter or leave the buildings while authorities investigated, school officials said. Deputies from the Macomb County Sheriff’s Office searched the high school and found nothing suspicious, but students were dismissed earlier than their usual dismissal time. The high school was one of several schools in the Metro Detroit area apparently targeted by pranksters on Tuesday, including two facilities in Ferndale where phony weapons were found, according to media reports. Police encourage parents, students, and community members to report any suspicious statements or activity to law enforcement.

Why Detroit cowboy brought his horse on a bus: ‘I’m everywhere with my horses’
articles.description: Urban City Cowboys, which originally started in Detroit, offers equestrian therapy for children with disabilities and rodeo lessons, including barrel racing, relay races and general horsemanship.
articles.content: It turns out Jordan Williams wasn’t actually trying to ride a Detroit bus with his horse Raven. Williams, cofounder of Urban City Cowboys, was out with his best friend (another horse owner), and their horses in Detroit over the weekend for a fundraiser, riding along 7 Mile Road, when he came across a Detroit Department of Transportation (DDOT) bus pulling into a stop. Williams said he spoke to the driver, jokingly remarked that the horse was his service animal and was on and off the bus in no time, much to the astonishment of a passenger inside who snapped some pictures. Williams didn’t know the person outside recording him — a video that would soon go viral — but he did intend to make a splash with the stunt. “I’m always known for doing stunts on my horses as well … I’m standing up on them, riding backwards, riding sideways,” Williams, 35, told the Detroit Free Press at his Romulus barn on Thursday, Nov. 12. Related: Watch two horses get on a Detroit bus Surveillance footage provided to the Free Press from the bus by the City of Detroit, including multiple angles in one video clip, shows the two riders at the stop. “If he can get in here, it is what it is,” a chuckling bus driver is heard saying in the 1:35 minute clip. “Hey, you want me to let them in?” It’s unclear what Williams and his friend say in response in the video, but the driver says “service animal” a few times. The ramp is lowered, as a passenger and the driver both smile and laugh. Williams brings Raven onto the bus followed by his friend and his horse, who then promptly exit out a side door near the back. “That’s crazy,” the driver says. A passenger can be heard saying, “We good.” The bus then rolls away, leaving the horses and their riders behind at the stop. Williams, who calls himself a cowboy and brings his horses to the city in a trailer, wanted to bring awareness to what he’s doing. Donate “I’m everywhere with my horses,” Williams said. The born-and-raised Detroiter moved to Romulus from the city last April to pursue his goal of running a farm for Detroit youth and a Western rodeo school. Urban City Cowboys, which originally started in Detroit, offers equestrian therapy for children with disabilities and rodeo lessons, including barrel racing, relay races and general horsemanship. For kids unable to compete in a rodeo, the program does a mock rodeo. He doesn’t work only with youth. He has a participant who is 5 years old and another who is 68, he said. “I was always an animal lover,” he said. He was 13, on the way home from school, when he came across horses at a funeral home. He asked a man there if he could ride, got some quick lessons and didn’t want to get off. That man, who called Williams a natural and would become his godfather, told him to call him the next day so he could talk to his parents about some lessons. Williams made that call at 6 a.m. “The rest is history,” he said. When he started doing rodeo, he realized nobody looked like him. Then he was introduced to the Black rodeo world and wanted to get involved. Williams sustains himself through horse rodeo earnings, takes his horses to events, does field trips and trail rides. He takes care of 10 horses belonging to other people, and has 12 of his own, including Raven, the rich brown American Paint Horse that boarded the bus. It was actually Raven’s first time in the city and “she did fantastic,” he said. The 12-year-old is his newest horse and a birthday gift. The second horse on the bus belongs to his friend. Williams’ sprawling property is home to more than horses. He’s got three dogs, a parrot, a snake, chickens, chicks, turkeys, geese, a cow, goats, an alpaca, pigs and barn cats. He has eggs from his free range chickens. On a brisk morning at his barn, a rooster crowed, ducks scurried about and a baby goat — 4-month-old Princess Fiona (like the “Shrek” character) — sidled over to a reporter’s feet. “Some days, it’s still unreal,” he said, dressed in a poncho and black cowboy hat. “It’s a lot of work, but it’s rewarding now. It’s like, ‘Ah, I’m doing what I want to do.’ I’m doing what I love. It finally came. I waited patiently, I worked hard and now here it is.” Williams owns 10 acres, a neighbor leases him another 10 and the city of Romulus, about 30 minutes from Detroit, allows him to use the nearby trails. It’s a big change from the city. Back when he was in Detroit, Williams transformed his garage into a barn for his horse. His neighbors were really nice about it, he said. He actually worked for Detroit Animal Control as an animal care technician. He was going to be an animal control officer but he realized he probably broke too many rules. He struggled to have farm animals in Detroit, he said. In an updated statement Thursday, the city of Detroit said that while DDOT welcomes service animals when they meet Americans with Disabilities Act requirements, the horses were apparently brought on the bus for other reasons. Alexis Ware, deputy director of media relations for the mayor’s office, said the city doesn’t typically comment on any disciplinary action, but that DDOT officials spoke to the bus driver, adding that everyone in the department will receive training to make sure they’re aware of the different policies. “We recognize that the actions in the video were meant to draw awareness to a positive cause. And we also acknowledge that this presented safety concerns for other passengers on public transit and for the horses themselves,” the statement said. The statement went on to say: “This is an opportunity to retrain DDOT bus operators and to educate our Detroit residents on everything that we are doing to guarantee safe, timely and high-quality service through DDOT. The City of Detroit also stands ready to assist our local entrepreneurs by connecting them with programs and opportunities that safely increase awareness of their organizations, and helps them expand their positive impact on our City.” Reach reporter Nushrat Rahman at nrahman@freepress.com.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.description: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.content: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.Read full article Comments

articles.title: ChatGPT’s new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you
articles.description: ChatGPT Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out on users' behalf, starting with a limited rollout to U.S. Pro subscribers.
articles.content: ChatGPT can now shop for you. On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots, help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf. The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express. OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs. In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction. The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks. While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app. Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf. It’s no surprise, then, that OpenAI would want to enter this space more with an agentic shopping feature of its own. To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant. The merchant will automatically receive what it needs to fulfill the order from the dot, like the shipping address and contact information, OpenAI says. The company notes that customers who shop via their dots will still be able to earn their credit card rewards and be able to take advantage of protections that typically come with cards, like being able to dispute transactions. The limited availability at launch will allow OpenAI to test and improve the feature and its capabilities before rolling it out more broadly. In the future, the company plans to offer users more control over the feature by allowing them to set spending limits or configure other parameters around purchase categories or time periods, so they can pre-approve purchases that their agent can then handle more autonomously. It also aims to make the agentic shopping feature an option at a broader number of supported retailers. This could be a challenge in some areas, where retailers are blocking AI agents from using their site; on the shopping front, the largest retailer to ban AI agents is Amazon, as it aims to steer users to its own AI agent, Alexa, instead. To help retailers adapt to agentic commerce, OpenAI also published a Commerce Partner Playbook that offers tools and guidance to sites that want to support customers using agents. articles.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
articles.description: Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia following an affair, which could have ramifications for national security as the U.S. and China race to develop the most advanced AI infrastructure.
articles.content: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. That same evening, Senator Tim Scott (R-SC) requested that Huang and Lutnick both testify before the Senate Banking Committee. “The American people deserve answers,” Scott wrote on X. After Huang was already ousted from Nvidia, we continued to learn more incriminating claims about the former CEO. According to Reuters, Huang had a third affair with an additional, unnamed employee of Nvidia. Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress, will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said. The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed. The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported. The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported. Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO. “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia, Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.” “Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote. Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day. Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.” U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report, U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information. The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump, has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China. Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.” “NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time. It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
articles.description: Heinz von Foerster thought population would grow exponentially and "squeeze" us all to death.
articles.content: As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point. It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus—one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever. Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. So he projected that human population growth would march inexorably toward infinity. We wouldn't starve to death; von Foerster thought we would be ingenious enough to solve the food supply problem. Instead, "they will be squeezed to death," he wrote.Read full article Comments

articles.title: ICE agents came to meatpacking country in Kansas. Then voters went to the polls
articles.content: DODGE CITY, Kan. (AP) — Jose Del Real looked over the crowd from the stage in a park, at hundreds of his neighbors with furious signs tucked under their arms, voicing their anger at immigration agents who had descended on their town and started rounding up their friends and family. His daughters, in the front row, were crying. Del Real, an Army veteran who served two tours in Iraq, hadn’t voted in a decade. He thought it wouldn’t matter in this ruby red corner of Kansas. But the midterm election was weeks away. He draped an American flag over his shoulders, put on his Iraq veteran cap and ended his speech with a message: “None of this matters if you do not vote. Let’s go vote.” Jose Del Real, a U.S. Army Veteran, poses for a photo in Dodge City, Kan., on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Nick Ingram) Photo made with a smartphone. Jose Del Real, a U.S. Army Veteran, poses for a photo in Dodge City, Kan., on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Nick Ingram) Photo made with a smartphone. They did. This county and two of its neighbors in southwestern Kansas, Republican strongholds where a steady stream of immigrants have settled over the decades to work at feed lots and slaughterhouses, swung wildly to the left. The shift helped elect a Democratic U.S. senator from Kansas for the first time in nearly a century, signaling the limits of President Donald Trump’s aggressive deportation agenda. Since Democrats won back control of Congress in a decisive rebuke to Republicans, Trump has sent mixed messages about how he plans to handle immigration enforcement going forward. He suggested that his approach to deportations was too harsh but also named hard-liner Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff. Both parties will be recalibrating their approach ahead of the next presidential campaign. Here in Kansas, late September raids ignited a maelstrom of rage, turning many who had been apathetic, like Del Real, into determined voters. Masked officers in tactical gear banged on doors before dawn. They stopped cars in the middle of intersections. Businesses shuttered. Families feared leaving their houses. Children stopped going to school. Some livestreamed themselves being detained. One man pleaded “God help me” in Spanish, his hands shaking, as he asked anyone watching to let his family know. The resistance came not only from Democrats or the Latino population, which has grown to about two-thirds of Dodge City. Kansas’ embattled Republican senator, Roger Marshall, who would lose his reelection bid to Adam Hamilton, issued a statement pleading with the administration to consult local officials before launching raids. Del Real regrets he didn’t vote in 2024, when Trump roared back into office pledging mass deportations. “We had to see it in front of us,” Del Real said. “I had to see it in the flesh.” The gates leading into Dodge City boast that it’s the “Queen of the Cowtowns.” Its main street is named after the classic Western set here, “Gunsmoke.” Murals celebrating cowboy history mix with evidence of a changing culture: storefronts showcasing quinceañera dresses, Mexican bakeries, city signs printed in both Spanish and English. Del Real’s family came from Mexico when he was a kindergartner. Like most here, they came to work. The area — Dodge City and the region’s other hubs, Garden City and Liberal — is known as the Golden Triangle of Meatpacking, responsible for about a quarter of the U.S. beef supply. Some here thought their importance to the nation’s food might spare them from the administration’s deportation campaigns, said Amy Soberanes, a 25-year-old local organizer. Soberanes, the daughter of Mexican immigrants, said she and others tried for years to get people — particularly their young, Latino neighbors — engaged. Community organizers Amy Soberanes, left, and Angelica Plata sit near the site of immigration enforcement protests in Dodge City, Kan., on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Claire Galofaro) Photo made with a smartphone. Community organizers Amy Soberanes, left, and Angelica Plata sit near the site of immigration enforcement protests in Dodge City, Kan., on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Claire Galofaro) Photo made with a smartphone. But, from rural Kansas, immigration raids in places like Minneapolis and Chicago felt abstract. Then they saw their own streets in social media videos. People were furious, said Soberanes, who worried the daily protests could get out of hand. They told people not to slash tires or break windows, to store up their anger and take it out on Election Day. “We’ll see them at the ballot box,” she recalls repeating. Her phone rang and rang. People she’d hassled to vote for years asked: How do I register? “If ICE hadn’t come, we would still be red, 100%,” she said. “And so I thank Donald Trump for sending immigration here.” No one knew immigration officers were coming. Dodge City Commissioner Rick Sowers said he and other city officials found out just like everyone else, through social media or masses of unmarked trucks on their neighbors’ lawns. They scrambled to get answers from the federal government – who they were looking for, who was in charge, how long they would stay – and never did. The Trump administration issued statements naming five “heinous criminals” they said had been arrested. But the Wichita Eagle dug into that claim and found none of those people were actually apprehended during the surge: Four had been deported months before and the fifth was already in prison, the newspaper found. The agency said it detained 104 people from southwest Kansas. Local officials have still never seen a list, Sowers said. Local Republican Chairman Scott Fischer, who describes himself as a supporter of strong borders, was surprised by the operation’s intensity. “There was a little showmanship,” he said. “I don’t know why it was like that.” GOP leader Scott Fischer talks about the meatpacking industry at a cattle auction facility in Dodge City, Kan., on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (AP Photo/Claire Galofaro) Photo made with a smartphone. GOP leader Scott Fischer talks about the meatpacking industry at a cattle auction facility in Dodge City, Kan., on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (AP Photo/Claire Galofaro) Photo made with a smartphone. He said he still considers the county red — it voted, narrowly, for Republican gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson. The Associated Press called that race Thursday: Masterson lost to Democrat Cindy Holscher. But some Dodge City Republicans abandoned the party in the U.S. Senate race. Dr. Russell Arben Fox, political science professor at Friends University in Wichita, said swings as dramatic as that one couldn’t have happened without some white, moderate Republicans changing their minds. More than half of Kansas voters in the Senate race disapprove of how ICE is handling its job, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. That’s consistent with the 61% of voters who say this nationally. Most of the Latino immigrants here are hard-working, family-oriented, faithful people – a perfect fit for conservative Kansas values, Fischer said, so local Republicans tend to have a nuanced view on immigration. Some public officials have for years begged the federal government for reforms to provide a pathway for these workers who run the region’s economy. “In general terms, mass deportation is not practical,” Fischer said. “When we say send them all home, what does that mean? Who is them?” To many here, “them” this time meant relatives and friends. In this small town, nearly everybody is connected to everybody else, so they did what they could to help. Oscar Soto delivered food to people afraid to leave home during the deportation raids. He started calling it “the black week,” after the black plague. That’s what it felt like to him, a pestilence that arrived suddenly. His mother came here from Mexico, he said, and though she is here legally, she was terrified. “It seemed unreal,” he said. “It was stuff that’s never been seen here, and it was day after day after day.” Oscar Soto works in his family-owned grocery story in Dodge City, Kan., on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (AP Photo/Claire Galofaro) Photo made with a smartphone. Oscar Soto works in his family-owned grocery story in Dodge City, Kan., on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (AP Photo/Claire Galofaro) Photo made with a smartphone. He works at a family-owned grocery, and strung a garland of flags from around the world above the counter when it opened. Most customers are from Mexico and Guatemala, he said, but he wanted to signal that the store was for everyone. Then he hung a big American flag from the ceiling. It means to him that anyone, from anywhere, can come here, work hard and build a life, free from fear. That belief in the American dream was shaken for him when ICE arrived. So he registered to vote for the first time at age 39. He stood in line to cast his ballot, amazed by how many young, Latino voters were waiting along with him. AP writers Nicholas Riccardi in Denver and Linley Sanders in Washington contributed.
