articles.title: Introducing ChatGPT Wallet
articles.description: Introducing ChatGPT Wallet, a secure way for agents in ChatGPT Work, Codex, and dots to complete purchases with user approval and existing card protections.
articles.content: Building trusted agentic payments with networks, banks, and businesses. We’re introducing ChatGPT Wallet, setting a new bar for secure payments by agents. It’s the first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes. Built in partnership with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa, ChatGPT Wallet will initially be available through dots for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US. Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re releasing tools and guidance to help businesses support customers using agents. 1.2B people use ChatGPT each week, and many of them turn to it to research products, compare options, and decide what to buy. With ChatGPT Wallet, we’re now helping people complete purchases, and giving their agents a way to pay that businesses can accept with their existing systems. To accept payment from ChatGPT Wallet, websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents. We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users, so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability. ChatGPT Wallet gives agents a secure way to pay on a user’s behalf. Users add a card once, then approve each purchase without re-entering their payment details. Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make. After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent. We’re building agent-led commerce to fit reliably into existing systems. Users keep their card’s existing rewards and protections for eligible disputes with businesses, for example when an item is defective. Banks and networks bring their expertise to evaluating transactions. Users transact directly with businesses, which keep their customer relationships and control over pricing, fulfillment, returns, and customer service. Over time, we expect users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases with enhanced safeguards that build on today’s protections, including biometric checks and clear records of authorization. Agentic commerce is still in its early days. As agents begin to take on more shopping and purchasing tasks, many websites and payment systems are still adapting to this modality. Some sites may unintentionally block purchases through ChatGPT Wallet or other agentic payment products, and we are focused on helping businesses make that transition. Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re publishing a Commerce Partner Playbook(opens in a new window) with tools and practical guidance to help businesses support customers using agents through their existing websites and systems. It covers making product information available, ensuring agent access, and working with payment and risk providers to reduce unnecessary declines. Businesses can start with the areas most relevant to their customers: Help customers find accurate product information. Claim your business in ChatGPT and, once verified, update your business details and upload a product feed with current pricing and availability. Ensure ChatGPT agents can access your website. Configure your CDN or firewall to recognize signed requests using Web Bot Auth and confirm your general site security measures are not inadvertently blocking ChatGPT agents. Browser access does not require a plugin or product feed. Work with your payments and risk providers to support agent purchases. Wallet’s payment tokens work with existing checkout flows, but risk systems may still flag legitimate purchases made by agents, leading to declines or cancellations. You can work with your providers to understand how they recognize these transactions. We’re also working with fraud prevention partners including Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd and payment service providers including Adyen, Checkout.com, and Stripe to help their systems recognize legitimate purchases made by agents. Give agents more ways to work with your business. Build a plugin to let agents check availability, manage carts, or take other actions through your existing systems. Websites can also add WebMCP tools. ChatGPT Wallet begins rolling out today in dots, enabling users to have their dot complete purchases on their behalf. It will initially be available to ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and older in the US with eligible US-issued cards. We’ll work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to learn from early use and expand availability, helping more customers and businesses benefit from agentic commerce.

articles.title: ElevenLabs’ new app combines meeting note-taking and dictation for teams
articles.content: In the last few months, Fireflies, Wispr Flow, and Granola have all released competing capabilities in the dictation and meeting note-taking space. The newest entrant in that category is voice AI giant ElevenLabs, which this week released an experimental app called ElevenAI that combines meeting note-taking, dictation, and agent integration. Launched during its 11/11 Summit in New York, ElevenAI is still in preview, and you have to sign up for early access instead of just downloading an app. ElevenLabs, valued at $22 billion, is very much positioning this as a product that lives within a team as compared to a productivity tool for an individual. ElevenAI packs all the features typically found in other apps in the category. It can take meeting notes across your meetings and notify other participants that the conversation is being recorded. Users can query data across meetings and get live assistance during a chat, helping them recall a key detail from older conversations. ElevenLabs also allows companies to integrate ElevenAgent and take follow-up actions such as writing a draft email based on meeting notes. Plus, there’s a dictation feature, which lets users convert speech to cleaned-up text in any app with support for over 90 languages. The company said that the app is capable of understanding industry-specific terms across dictation and meeting transcription. ElevenAI allows the company to use its own model as a showcase and also utilize its agent platforms for better context funneling. The startup’s positioning might not be to directly compete in the productivity market, but rather to give enterprise teams an option to not buy licenses to a notetaker and use its solution instead. All meeting-related tools are rushing to become central knowledge hubs for companies while aiming to automate knowledge extraction and follow-up actions In the last week, the company also launched its v3 series of Scribe speech-to-text models with live transcription capabilities and the ability for companies to fine-tune models using their own data, a tool to pick the right language model based on use case, and a routine creator that automates tasks based on the transcript. articles.title: Claude’s Duet agent is a little neurotic and surprisingly helpful
articles.description: Let’s get to work. | Photo: Allison Johnson / The Verge Normally, the products I test don't offer to help me write up my experience with them. Duet is different. Claude Duet is Anthropic's AI agent for consumers, the latest attempt by an AI company to try to convince us that agents can be useful for people who don't write code. It's been an interesting couple of months: Instinct gave us an impressive text-based assis
articles.content: Normally, the products I test don’t offer to help me write up my experience with them. Duet is different. Claude Duet is Anthropic’s AI agent for consumers, the latest attempt by an AI company to try to convince us that agents can be useful for people who don’t write code. It’s been an interesting couple of months: Instinct gave us an impressive text-based assistant, Meta offered us its cute little guy, Muse, to help us buy things, and OpenAI gave us the more work-oriented Dots. Claude Duet is even more focused on work than those. It’s also more consumer-friendly than Claude Cowork, which was more consumer-friendly than Claude Code — the coding agent that kicked off a whole hype cycle earlier this year. I’ve been testing it over the past week as I navigate a busy travel and work schedule. At turns it has been truly useful, kind of a nag, and very eager to write about itself. Duet is still a “research preview” according to Anthropic, and access is limited to Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers in the US, with a waitlist to join. It’s not here to order you burritos, either; it’s for “professionals and small business owners” and is meant to use its judgment about what needs your attention most. Like Meta’s Muse, Duet has its own app. (If you’re keeping score at home, yes, it has been updated to fully support the iPhone Duo). Duet uses Claude’s characteristically cheery, minimalist design. The app is consumer-friendly and approachable. Once you’ve connected all the productivity and chat services you want, it’ll look for ways to help out with and suggest them as cards you can swipe left or right to hide or accept — kind of a to-do list Tinder. In the name of testing, I went all in on Duet and gave it everything: my work email, calendar, Google Docs, and Slack. This gave it plenty of grist for the mill in more ways than I’d even realized at first. Because our biweekly staff meeting is automatically summarized in an email from Gemini, and Duet had access to my email, it was able to connect the dots between something said in a meeting and a direct message in Slack. Duet also worked out who my boss is because we have a shared Google Doc for our weekly 1:1 meetings. AI is at its most useful when it can suck up lots of data, and Duet wasted no time doing so. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_3369.png?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/IMG_3417.png?quality=90&strip=all] Duet has started each morning by greeting me with a brief message and some quick highlights for my day, like reminding me to pack an item required for a video shoot before my flight. Below that, it would suggest to-dos, usually ending in an offer to help draft a message or add an item to an agenda. This has often been helpful, though it sometimes felt like interacting with a slightly neurotic personal assistant. In one instance, I’d emailed someone I interviewed for a story that the article was likely to go up on Tuesday and that I’d send a link when it did. I submitted my draft to my editors late at night on Monday, and Tuesday morning Duet was beside itself. It wasn’t quite 9AM yet when it pointed out that the story was still waiting for an edit and I needed to get on that — or else I wouldn’t be able to send the link I promised. The concern was a bit misplaced. And it didn’t pick up on the nuance in my message implying that this was not a hard deadline, nor the fact that it was only 7AM local time for my editor. In other cases, it was surprisingly helpful. In planning out the next few weeks I’d missed the fact that upcoming time off would only leave me with a couple of working days before another big draft was due. Duet proposed a solution, offered to update the Google Doc with weekly notes for my editor, and drafted a Slack message for him noting the update. Reader, the message was a little too good. It copied my millennial habit of writing in all lowercase — which it pointed out in a slightly self-congratulatory aside — and used an abbreviation we often use to refer to our CMS. But it also shortened the word “signature” to “sig,” which I never would and made me laugh out loud. In any case, there’s no fooling anyone; the Slack message was tagged with a “sent with Claude” label. Duet often volunteered to help start my drafts, which is always a hard no for me. I’ll type up my own little blogs, thank you very much Claude. If you’re not a writer, I can see how taking care of little writing chores here and there would be helpful. But this started feeling like a Spider-Man-pointing-at-Spider-Man moment when the task it wanted to help with was reviewing itself. It was a little uncanny, too. Even setting aside the fact that I was writing about Duet, it’s kind of weird knowing that it can read every email, draft, and Slack I send. It can read all of that because I opted in to sharing that data, and I knew full well what I was doing. But it’s another thing to see it in practice. I wonder if it would change how I work if I knew I didn’t really need to take responsibility for putting things on my calendar, writing down a to-do list, or paying attention in a meeting because Duet will just handle it. Maybe that’s how CEOs live. Not that I cherish creating calendar entries, but I wonder if I would end up feeling a bit disconnected from my workplace. I don’t think Duet or any other AI agent is quite ready to make us feel like we’re all the CEOs of our own little worlds. There’s a key word in the title “personal assistant”: personal. A person can pick up on nuances in tone to understand what’s a big deal and what isn’t. A person will pick up on communication norms and deploy them sensibly. A person can be tactful. Anthropic’s blog post mentions that the company is continuing to “test its judgment about when to message you,” so it’s possible Duet will calibrate a little better over time. But AI overall isn’t good at understanding nuance or tone, and it’s not clear if it ever will be. For me, Duet made it a little more clear what I want AI to do for me and what I don’t. Communication happens all over the place in a modern workplace — in emails, DMs, meetings, shared docs. Having AI find discrepancies that have been overlooked between all of these sources and point them out proactively is really helpful. I like it as a backstop for my own organizational systems, not as a replacement for them. I don’t like it in the creative process. Like, at all. I want to find “my own ways into and around a topic,” as Hank Green said of his own reliance on AI. If you send a robot to do the legwork, you miss the opportunity to stumble across something unexpected. It’s part of what makes the work enjoyable. And I’m certainly not about to let an agent review itself for me. You hear that, Duet?

Open source TTS vs paid APIs: How to choose wisely
articles.description: Compare open source TTS vs paid APIs on cost, control, licensing, and data residency, and learn how to evaluate models before you commit.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Neither open source nor paid text to speech (TTS) APIs are inherently better than the other. Each is a viable solution to different use cases and business needs. Paid APIs incur regular subscription or workload costs. Free and open source TTS shifts the costs to running additional infrastructure and the developer and engineering time to maintain it. This article offers an unbiased take on open source TTS vs paid APIs, explores when each option is appropriate, and demonstrates how to evaluate TTS models, free or paid, to find the one best suited to your needs. Open source text to speech (TTS) and paid APIs can both work well for different use cases. Models of all types are mature enough now that both design approaches can deliver sufficient speech quality. Which approach is best is more determined by your team’s capacity and the scale of your workload. Open source and self-hosted TTS typically offers more control over the full stack. You don’t pay per character, but you do pay for the compute infrastructure and for the staff to manage that infrastructure and model code. Self-hosting supports data sovereignty. Text and audio can stay completely local. Nothing needs to traverse the public internet, and all TTS operations stay within your jurisdiction and on the infrastructure you choose. This can be important or strictly required in sectors such as healthcare, finance, and government. Self-hosting gives you direct access to the full architecture from bare metal on up. You can fully optimize internal runtimes. You have full experimental control over the model weights and the inference pipeline, and you can customize the vocabulary. Accessing TTS through managed APIs is a turnkey solution. The infrastructure is preconfigured and available when you need it, backed by clear SLAs and running on scalable, multi-region cloud infrastructure. You just need to integrate your application to it via REST or WebSocket. Commercial APIs are also a common way to access the newest, high-parameter foundation models, which can deliver speech with natural prosody. If your goal is to accelerate your time to market using enterprise-grade resources, then a managed API may be the better choice. The trade-off is that you pay metered, per-character rates. Some teams self-host only to control where their data goes. Managed APIs can meet that need too, but the options may be limited to Enterprise plans, as is the case with ElevenLabs. For data residency, ElevenAPI stores customer data in the US by default. Enterprise customers can get isolated environments in the EU, India, and Singapore. Each is a fully separate workspace with its own URL, account, and API key. Residency controls storage only: processing can still happen outside the region through affiliates, subprocessors, support, and moderation, which the data processing agreement covers. For EU environments with Zero Retention Mode on, processing also stays in the EU, except for optional integrations such as custom LLMs or some post-call webhooks. Some products aren’t available in isolated environments. Zero Retention Mode (ZRM) deletes the inputs and outputs of eligible API requests as soon as each request finishes, and the requesting account’s email isn’t logged. It covers API traffic only, never the web UI. Eligible products include text to speech (including WebSocket), Text to Dialogue, Voice Changer, Speech to Text, Forced Alignment, Sound Effects, Music, and ElevenAgents. articles.title: Why a Detroit cowboy brought his horse aboard a DDOT bus
articles.description: Urban City Cowboys, which originally started in Detroit, offers equestrian therapy for children with disabilities and rodeo lessons, including barrel racing, relay races and general horsemanship.
articles.content: Detroit Free Press is a partner and shares a reporter with BridgeDetroit. Stories shared are not under a paywall. Detroit Free Press It turns out Jordan Williams wasn’t actually trying to ride a Detroit bus with his horse Raven. Williams, cofounder of Urban City Cowboys, was out with his best friend (another horse owner), and their horses in Detroit over the weekend for a fundraiser, riding along 7 Mile Road, when he came across a Detroit Department of Transportation (DDOT) bus pulling into a stop. Williams said he spoke to the driver, jokingly remarked that the horse was his service animal and was on and off the bus in no time, much to the astonishment of a passenger inside who snapped some pictures. Williams didn’t know the person outside recording him — a video that would soon go viral — but he did intend to make a splash with the stunt. “I’m always known for doing stunts on my horses as well … I’m standing up on them, riding backwards, riding sideways,” Williams, 35, told the Detroit Free Press at his Romulus barn on Thursday, Nov. 12. Surveillance footage provided to the Free Press from the bus by the City of Detroit, including multiple angles in one video clip, shows the two riders at the stop. “If he can get in here, it is what it is,” a chuckling bus driver is heard saying in the 1:35 minute clip. “Hey, you want me to let them in?” It’s unclear what Williams and his friend say in response in the video, but the driver says “service animal” a few times. The ramp is lowered, as a passenger and the driver both smile and laugh. Williams brings Raven onto the bus followed by his friend and his horse, who then promptly exit out a side door near the back. “That’s crazy,” the driver says. A passenger can be heard saying, “We good.” The bus then rolls away, leaving the horses and their riders behind at the stop. Williams, who calls himself a cowboy and brings his horses to the city in a trailer, wanted to bring awareness to what he’s doing. “I’m everywhere with my horses,” Williams said. The born-and-raised Detroiter moved to Romulus from the city last April to pursue his goal of running a farm for Detroit youth and a Western rodeo school. Urban City Cowboys, which originally started in Detroit, offers equestrian therapy for children with disabilities and rodeo lessons, including barrel racing, relay races and general horsemanship. For kids unable to compete in a rodeo, the program does a mock rodeo. He doesn’t work only with youth. He has a participant who is 5 years old and another who is 68, he said. “I was always an animal lover,” he said. He was 13, on the way home from school, when he came across horses at a funeral home. He asked a man there if he could ride, got some quick lessons and didn’t want to get off. That man, who called Williams a natural and would become his godfather, told him to call him the next day so he could talk to his parents about some lessons. Williams made that call at 6 a.m. “The rest is history,” he said. When he started doing rodeo, he realized nobody looked like him. Then he was introduced to the Black rodeo world and wanted to get involved. Williams sustains himself through horse rodeo earnings, takes his horses to events, does field trips and trail rides. He takes care of 10 horses belonging to other people, and has 12 of his own, including Raven, the rich brown American Paint Horse that boarded the bus. It was actually Raven’s first time in the city and “she did fantastic,” he said. The 12-year-old is his newest horse and a birthday gift. The second horse on the bus belongs to his friend. Williams’ sprawling property is home to more than horses. He’s got three dogs, a parrot, a snake, chickens, chicks, turkeys, geese, a cow, goats, an alpaca, pigs and barn cats. He has eggs from his free range chickens. On a brisk morning at his barn, a rooster crowed, ducks scurried about and a baby goat — 4-month-old Princess Fiona (like the “Shrek” character) — sidled over to a reporter’s feet. “Some days, it’s still unreal,” he said, dressed in a poncho and black cowboy hat. “It’s a lot of work, but it’s rewarding now. It’s like, ‘Ah, I’m doing what I want to do.’ I’m doing what I love. It finally came. I waited patiently, I worked hard and now here it is.” Williams owns 10 acres, a neighbor leases him another 10 and the city of Romulus, about 30 minutes from Detroit, allows him to use the nearby trails. It’s a big change from the city. Back when he was in Detroit, Williams transformed his garage into a barn for his horse. His neighbors were really nice about it, he said. He actually worked for Detroit Animal Control as an animal care technician. He was going to be an animal control officer but he realized he probably broke too many rules. He struggled to have farm animals in Detroit, he said. In an updated statement Thursday, the city of Detroit said that while DDOT welcomes service animals when they meet Americans with Disabilities Act requirements, the horses were apparently brought on the bus for other reasons. Alexis Ware, deputy director of media relations for the mayor’s office, said the city doesn’t typically comment on any disciplinary action, but that DDOT officials spoke to the bus driver, adding that everyone in the department will receive training to make sure they’re aware of the different policies. “We recognize that the actions in the video were meant to draw awareness to a positive cause. And we also acknowledge that this presented safety concerns for other passengers on public transit and for the horses themselves,” the statement said. The statement went on to say: “This is an opportunity to retrain DDOT bus operators and to educate our Detroit residents on everything that we are doing to guarantee safe, timely and high-quality service through DDOT. The City of Detroit also stands ready to assist our local entrepreneurs by connecting them with programs and opportunities that safely increase awareness of their organizations, and helps them expand their positive impact on our City.” Reach reporter Nushrat Rahman at nrahman@freepress.com.

articles.title: This time, rural voters ‘just weren’t there’ for the GOP
articles.description: LAMPASAS, Texas — Standing at the edge of his family’s 300-acre cattle ranch in Central Texas, Clayton Tucker is characteristically attired in a white Stetson western hat, a beige shirt with pearl snaps, and lightly faded Wrangler jeans. At 35, Tucker is poised to become the first Democrat in more than three decades to serve […]
articles.content: Clayton Tucker, elected last week as Texas agriculture commissioner, poses at his ranch in Lampasas, Texas. Tucker is the first Democrat in more than three decades to hold the position. Across the country, rural voters — staunchly Republican in recent decades — either defected to Democrats or stayed home. (Photo by David Montgomery/Stateline)LAMPASAS, Texas — Standing at the edge of his family’s 300-acre cattle ranch in Central Texas, Clayton Tucker is characteristically attired in a white Stetson western hat, a beige shirt with pearl snaps, and lightly faded Wrangler jeans. At 35, Tucker is poised to become the first Democrat in more than three decades to serve as Texas agriculture commissioner, a post from which he will oversee policies affecting much of rural Texas. The last Democrat to serve as agriculture commissioner left office in January of 1991— a month before Tucker was born. Tucker, who takes office in January, benefitted from the Democratic wave that swept across Texas and other states in the midterm elections, propelled by widespread disenchantment with Republican policies, both in the cities and on the farm. Across the country, rural voters — staunchly Republican in recent decades — either defected to Democrats or stayed home to protest the spread of data centers, rising fuel prices, the war in Iran and other grievances. In Texas, about 90% of the counties where turnout decreased were rural, according to The Texas Tribune. While many rural voters stayed faithful to GOP candidates, their diminished numbers at the polls helped clear the way for Democratic victories: In the state’s U.S. Senate race, the Democrats improved their performance in all 254 Texas counties, compared with the 2024 U.S. Senate contest. “People felt like they were being treated as sacrificial lambs for Wall Street, for Silicon Valley, for all these tech bros and oligarchs and everyone else,” Tucker said in an interview behind the steering wheel of his parked 1982 GMC pickup truck, “and they just weren’t being supported by our government anymore.” Rural disenchantment also helped drive epic Democratic victories in other states. In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton was elected to the U.S. Senate, the first Kansas Democrat to win a Senate seat since 1932. Analysts attributed Hamilton’s victory to a rural backlash over high fuel and fertilizer prices and cheap imported beef. In Montana, former smoke-jumper Sam Forstag flipped one of the state’s two congressional seats, becoming the first Montana Democrat to win a U.S. House seat since 1994. Partisan control also shifted in Iowa, where agriculture-related jobs employ roughly 1 in 5 residents. Iowa Democrats won the governor’s race, a U.S. Senate seat and three of the state’s four congressional seats. Republicans maintained their grip on both chambers of the state legislature, but Democrats narrowed the gap. Iowa Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson won just over half of rural and small-town voters in her unsuccessful bid for one of Iowa’s U.S. Senate seats, according to The Associated Press. But that was a smaller percentage of rural and small-town voters than the GOP got in 2022, and the diminished margin helped secure a victory for Democratic candidate Josh Turek. “It was a setback for Republicans and now they have to figure out how they’re going to get back some of the voters they probably lost,” said Abhishek Chatterjee, an associate professor of political science at the University of Montana. Texas the epicenter Texas, the nation’s second-largest state, was an epicenter of the midterm upheaval. Voters there turned against three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott to choose state Rep. Gina Hinojosa as the state’s first Latina governor and the first Democrat to hold the office since Ann Richards left in 1995. Texas voters also elected Democratic state Rep. James Talarico to the U.S. Senate and placed Democrats, including Tucker, in all of the top statewide offices. Democrats also took over the Texas House, which has been controlled by Republicans since 2003. Republicans still hold the majority in the Texas Senate and are considering rule changes to undercut the power of incoming presiding officer Vikki Goodwin, a Democratic legislator who defeated incumbent Republican Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick for the state’s number two post, which includes leadership of the legislature’s upper chamber. In the aftermath of what she called a “nationwide Republican defeat,” Texas Republican Party Chair D’rinda Randall announced the formation of an invitation-only Texas Mandate Committee composed of statewide leaders charged with “examining what occurred and developing a strategy to win Texas back.” “This is not about placing blame,” she said in a statement. “It is about planning to win.” Kendall Scudder, chair of the Texas Democratic Party as well as the Democratic National Committee’s Rural Council, told Stateline that his party’s Texas triumph resulted in part from a concentrated campaign that included a heavy focus on rural Texas. “What I think happened was folks in rural Texas gave Democrats an opportunity to state our case, and we hadn’t had that in while,” said Scudder, who grew up in Sulphur Springs in largely rural East Texas. “I think we started making inroads, and part of that could be because Republicans weren’t worth showing up and voting for. But I think another piece is that Democrats were talking about things that were important to rural Texas.” Top issues that resonated strongly in rural Texas, he said, included the spread of data centers, “mass surveillance” by mounted Flock cameras that read license plates, and inadequate funding for state schools. As result, he said, 21 largely rural counties that voted red in previous elections “went blue this time.” “I think we moved the needle in a good way, and I think if Democrats deliver for those communities, we can start to unlock more and more gains,” he said. Outgoing Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller, a Republican who lost his primary race for re-election, echoed Tucker and Scudder’s assertions that rural voters are up in arms over data centers, artificial intelligence, Flock cameras, and soaring fuel prices. Tucker says he will push for a moratorium on data centers after he takes office in January. “We’ve never had any real property tax relief,” Miller said in a phone interview “Diesel’s the highest it’s ever been. Fertilizer’s the highest it’s ever been. I don’t think the Democrats took anything away from the Republicans,” Miller said, “we basically gave it to them.” Miller put much of the blame for rural dissension on Abbott’s policies. Abbott endorsed Miller’s Republican primary opponent, Nate Sheets, who in turn was beaten by Tucker in the general election. A $1 billion publicly funded private school voucher program that Abbott pushed through the Texas Legislature in 2025 also stirred dissent in parts of rural Texas, amid fears that it will siphon money from public schools. “There was a lot of hard feelings about the voucher program out there,” said Snapper Carr of Austin, a managing partner and general counsel of Focused Advocacy, a lobbying firm that represents cities and communities throughout the state. The Republican downturn, he said, was particularly evident in what he said are typically “bright red areas of West Texas,” where residents “talk about the price of diesel like we all talk about the weather.” “The Republicans still carried them,” he said, “but their margins were much less than what they’ve been in the past…There was a large number of past Republicans that didn’t show up this time.” ‘Totally surprised’ In Briggs, an unincorporated Central Texas community with around 100 residents, Ray Bizzell, 83, offered his thoughts on the election outcome as he left Sunday’s services at the Briggs Baptist Church. Bizzell, who runs a floor covering business about 20 miles away in Georgetown, Texas, said he voted “Republican, straight ticket” and “was totally surprised” by Democrats’ strong showing in the state. “I really thought we might hold it,” he said. “I just think my beliefs align better with the Republican Party.” In Williamson County, which stretches from the high-growth Austin suburbs to patches of rural Texas further east, the unexpected Democratic surge propelled first-time candidate Chris Jimenez, 42, into a state legislative victory over a Republican incumbent backed the governor. In this year’s U.S. Senate race, Williamson County swung nearly 19 points toward the Democrats compared with the Senate race in 2024, according to The Associated Press. Jimenez, who lives on a pecan farm with his wife and 16-year-old daughter near the town of Elgin, is headed to the statehouse after defeating Republican state Rep. Caroline Harris Davila for the House seat once held by Talarico. Jimenez’s opponent was endorsed by Abbott. Jimenez grew up on a ranch near Sanderson and served in the Marine Corps. He said his thoughts of running for office intensified after he was “pulled over and profiled by a police officer,” he told Stateline. “I was very concerned on multiple levels. I figured, ‘Hey, if this is happening to me, a Marine Corps veteran just trying to make my life here on the farm, it’s got to be happening to multiple people.’” “Did I expect to win? I felt our message resonated with people, regardless of their political affiliation,” he said. “It was never about being red or blue. It was about survival in Texas and it’s gotten hard for a lot of folks.” Jimenez has joined other incoming lawmakers in pre-filing bills before the January start of the legislature. His measure call for repealing “the private school voucher scheme,” eliminating a sales tax exemption for data centers and expanding Medicaid benefits in Texas. Republican data analyst Derek Ryan said Republicans needed to win by “a very large margin” in rural counties to counter strong turnout in predominately Democratic urban areas. The GOP only had 32-point advantage in those counties in this year’s mid-term elections, he said, compared to 55 points in 2022 and 46 points in 2018. Ryan estimated that about 625,000 Republicans sat out the election, according to the Texas Rural Report. “We knew there was going to be a slight shift towards the Democrats in rural Texas,” Ryan told Stateline. “I didn’t think it was going to be this significant, but it comes down to the economy and gas prices. “When you live in rural Texas, it’s a long drive anywhere you go. So when it’s costing you more to fill up your tank, you know you’re going to vote with that in mind.” Suzanne Bellsnyder, who owns and runs a newspaper in the small town of Spearman near the Oklahoma state line, said she has analyzed all 184 Texas counties with a population under 50,000 and found signs of Republican slippage in areas that have typically served as Republican bulwarks. “Republicans have always depended on the rural counties to kind of be their firewall, their insurance policy,” she said. But this time, she added, “they just weren’t there.” This story was originally produced by Stateline, which is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network which includes Michigan Advance, and is supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.

El-Sayed (D-Ann Arbor) previously said he would support Van Hollen if he sought the leadership position of the caucus. As the Democrats regained control of the U.S. Senate in the Nov. 3 election, it was unclear if someone would challenge Schumer, who has led the caucus since 2017. In an interview with Michigan Advance, El-Sayed reaffirmed his support on Thursday afternoon, hours before Van Hollen jumped into the race. “I was the first to be calling on him as the next leader, so I would love to see him run, and I’d love to see him as our next leader,” El-Sayed said. Following Van Hollen’s announcement, El-Sayed said in a news release that Michiganders rejected “the failed status quo and the politics that too often leaves families behind” when they voted last week to give Democrats a majority in Congress. “But we need to earn our mandate. That demands new leadership,” he said in a statement. “Senator Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus.” U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen speaks at a rally for U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Ferndale, Mich., on July 25, 2026. U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren and U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal also spoke at the event. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance) U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) also has called for new leadership for the Democratic caucus, but she has not publicly backed Van Hollen. Slotkin said she is not actively seeking the position. Schumer said Tuesday he’s “confident” he will be reelected as Democratic leader for the next Congress. The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers said in a news release that it also supports Van Hollen. “He’s a proven champion of working people who will fight to unrig an economy stacked against working families,” IAM President Brian Bryant said in a statement. “Senator Van Hollen understands this is a fight of Workers vs. Billionaires, and has the courage to deliver the change voters demanded. Workers did their part on election night. Now it’s Senate Democrats’ turn. Senator Van Hollen is the right choice.”

Detroit residents urge delay as city council advances RenCen redevelopment agreement
articles.description: DETROIT – City council members advanced an agreement between developers and residents tied to a $2.2 billion plan to transform Detroit’s Renaissance Center and surrounding East Riverfront into a residential and entertainment district. In a 2-1 vote, the City Council’s Planning and Economic Development Committee voted to send the community benefits agreement to the full council […]
articles.content: Teron Haynes Jr. was amongst the protestors demanding that the city council delay its Nov. 12, 2026, vote on the $43.5 million community benefits agreement. He is the only member of the NAC who didn't approve the agreement. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)DETROIT – City council members advanced an agreement between developers and residents tied to a $2.2 billion plan to transform Detroit’s Renaissance Center and surrounding East Riverfront into a residential and entertainment district. In a 2-1 vote, the City Council’s Planning and Economic Development Committee voted to send the community benefits agreement to the full council without a recommendation. Committee Chair Latisha Johnson said sending the agreement to the full council would allow members to raise additional questions and concerns during a public discussion. “If we determine that we’re not ready to move forward, then we know how to address that in the committee of the whole,” Johnson said. Councilmember Gabriela Santiago-Romero opposed advancing the agreement, saying she wanted more time to review the proposal and ensure questions raised by council members and residents are answered. “People don’t move to cities for their downtowns. They move to cities because of their transportation, their neighborhoods, their culture, their people, all of that,” Santiago-Romero said. “That’s what I’m trying to make sure that we have at the forefront here and this does feel very, very rushed.” Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield joined members of the project’s nine-member Neighborhood Advisory Council at a press conference on Nov. 5, where they signed the CBA, which dedicates $15 million to housing, $10 million to small businesses, $8 million to a community hub, $6 million to workforce development and education, and $4.5 million to parking, totaling $43.5 million. Developers also pledged an additional $90 million in voluntary payments in lieu of taxes or “PILOT” payments over 30 years, bringing the total announced commitments to $133.5 million. Dozens of residents, community organizers and business owners urged the city council to delay its vote on the community benefits agreement and give the community more time to provide input. “There are things that we have asked for over the last 10 weeks and all of a sudden they have disappeared out of the CBA,” said Nicole Small, of Save the RenCen, during a rally outside of the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center Thursday morning. “This is not a community benefits agreement, this is a developer benefits agreement. The mayor should be outraged. City Council should be outraged and the people of Detroit should definitely be outraged,” Small said. Protestors chanted “Whose riverfront? Our riverfront!” during a rally outside of the Coleman A. Young Municipal center on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance) The agreement is part of the city’s Community Benefits Ordinance, which requires developers of large-scale projects to engage residents who could be affected by the development. The Neighborhood Advisory Council is responsible for representing residents throughout that process. Its nine members include three City Council appointees, four appointees from the city’s Planning and Development Department and two elected neighborhood representatives. Still, some residents felt that they were left out of the process, especially after released text messages between council members showed they agreed not to make public the recordings or transcripts from closed negotiations with developers, at least until after the council voted to approve the CBA. “We got two months of public input on this process for a project that’s about to exist for the next 50 years,” said Jeremiah Wheeler of Detroit Action during the rally. “The money is coming from all around the city but the benefits are not going all around the city. The benefits are limited to … downtown and that’s not acceptable,” Wheeler said. Not every member of the NAC is in support of the agreement. Teron Haynes Jr. was the only council member who didn’t sign the CBA. “Those buildings don’t look obsolete to me. They’re standing and I’m not waiting for them to collapse,” Haynes said during the rally, pointing to the Renaissance Center. “We shouldn’t be waiting for Detroit to collapse either but that’s what’s going to happen if we keep giving billionaires this money and not investing into the community.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The agreement follows weeks of negotiations between the council and developers Bedrock Detroit and General Motors. During Thursday’s committee meeting, officials described it as the largest community benefits agreement in Detroit’s history. “We have community benefits in the agreement but the reason why I voted no was because I did not think that the benefits were substantial enough for, what we are giving to these developers but also what people in Detroit … have missed out on in the past decade as far as community development and investment,” Haynes told the Michigan Advance. The project calls for the demolition of two of the complex’s five towers, with plans to convert the remaining three into 934 mixed-income housing units and office space. Additional plans include a marina, an observation deck and 18 acres of proposed civic space across the broader 46-acre development site. Bedrock and GM are expected to invest more than $1.6 billion in the project, while the Downtown Development Authority will contribute $75 million. The remaining $505 million is expected to come through debt. Developers are also seeking more than $473 million in tax breaks over 30 years. Additional commercial tax incentives would bring the total requested subsidies to approximately $548 million. If approved by Detroit City Council, demolition work is expected to begin next summer. The project is expected to take at least 10 years to complete. City Council members are aiming to approve the plan before Thanksgiving, when the council will go on recess until next year. Billionaire Dan Gilbert, who founded Bedrock, pledged an additional $1 billion to establish a new nonprofit organization dedicated to redeveloping and operating the Renaissance Center and East Riverfront. Despite the donation, protesters said they would rather the new development be publicly owned and that there be more investment into developing housing throughout the city instead of downtown. “If the word philanthropy meant anything, then he (Dan Gilbert) would pay property taxes,” said Russ Bellant, of Detroiters for Tax Justice during Thursday morning’s protest. “Why isn’t he using those tax benefits that he’s looting from us … for an investment instead of coming back to us and saying, ‘Let me screw you for another half a billion dollars.’” Bedrock is the largest private property owner in Detroit, operating roughly 100 properties, most of them in the downtown area. Dozens of community leaders, advocates and residents spoke during public comment at Thursday’s Planning and Economic Development Committee meeting, with many urging council members to delay the proposed Renaissance Center redevelopment and give the community more time to weigh in on the project. Despite commenters being limited to 45 seconds, the meeting lasted more than five hours. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance) The redevelopment has drawn both support and concern from residents. Some question whether the project represents another major investment in downtown Detroit while neighborhoods elsewhere in the city continue to grapple with vacant lots and deteriorating homes. Another major concern, especially early in the community benefits process, was that the estimated area of impact was too small and did not include residents in surrounding areas. The Renaissance Center, located along Woodward Avenue in the city’s downtown area, is in District 5. Developers estimate that nearly 4,700 residents live in the impacted area. “The NAC should have considered bus riders who use Jefferson as a route. If this project goes through without any consideration, it would jeopardize access to jobs, access to city and county services and transit connections across Detroit and our county,” said Renard Munchinski, an organizer with Detroit People’s Platform, during virtual public comment at Thursday’s committee meeting. Supporters view the development as an investment in Detroit’s future. “In TechTown we see every day that local entrepreneurs don’t lack talent. They lack affordable storefronts, capital and coaching and this CBA delivers all three,” said Ned Staebler, President and CEO of TechTown. Ryan Sullivan, CEO of the Detroit Riverfront Conservancy also spoke in support of the project and urged the committee to pass the agreement. The project marks a significant turning point for one of Detroit’s most recognizable landmarks. The Renaissance Center opened in 1977, featuring a 73-story central hotel tower surrounded by four office towers. Two additional office towers opened in 1981. General Motors purchased the entire complex in 1996 for $73 million and established its global corporate headquarters there. But as hybrid work schedules became more common following the COVID-19 pandemic and office occupancy declined, GM announced in 2024 that it would relocate its global headquarters to Hudson’s Detroit, another Bedrock development. The 49-story skyscraper was also developed by the Detroit-based real estate firm, owned by billionaire Dan Gilbert. GM’s planned departure raised questions about the future of the Renaissance Center. Now, those questions have evolved into a multibillion-dollar redevelopment proposal that could reshape Detroit’s riverfront for decades. 5:51 pmThis story has been corrected to note that the vote by council was 2-1 and not 3-2 as originally reported.

Shield helps technicians hand off legacy portal work with OpenAI
articles.description: Shield uses OpenAI to help IT technicians hand off work in legacy portals. Its Forge agents navigate systems so technicians can focus on issues needing their judgment.
articles.content: With GPT‑6 Astra, the agents in Shield’s Forge platform navigate legacy portals so technicians can focus on issues that need their attention. For many small and medium-sized businesses, an outsourced IT services provider handles everything from an employee locked out of their laptop to a misconfigured firewall that took the office offline. Shield built Forge(opens in a new window), an AI operating system for IT services providers. The platform brings together business data and customer context to help providers complete IT support tasks end to end. That means its agents also need to work in the older portals technicians use every day. With OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra, Shield can now hand supported browser tasks to agents instead of leaving a technician to log in and finish them manually. “If a customer is locked out of their computer or there’s a phishing attack, speed is paramount,” says Jain. “Whether you’re going to solve their issue or you’re going to escalate to a human, you want to do either as fast as possible.” Before using GPT‑6 Astra, Forge’s agents could get stuck at systems they could not access. Customers then had to wait for a technician to complete that step. Shield tried computer use, where an AI model reads the screen, clicks, and types, with earlier models. Jain says they were not reliable or fast enough. “Usually, a system that doesn’t have an API is an old-school system that also doesn’t look very nice and is very hard to use, even by a human,” Jain says. Technicians spend much of their day in portals that manage tickets, devices and software licenses. Many of those systems lack APIs, so an agent needs to navigate the screen much as a person would. Forge’s AI Engineer assigns the work to a computer-use agent, and GPT‑6 Astra navigates the interface to complete supported tasks. Technicians decide which actions it can take on its own and where they need to review or approve the work. Shield says these browser workflows are live, with thousands of runs each month across its IT providers. Phone calls, on-site work and remote-desktop tasks still need human involvement. “GPT‑6 Astra allows our agents to embody what a technician does by logging into portals and legacy websites that might not have API access and performing tasks that only a human could six months ago,” says Mayank Jain, Head of Technology at Shield. Jain says GPT‑6 Astra was 35-40% faster on average than the legacy models Shield had used for computer-use tasks. He also says customer satisfaction is higher on tickets where AI is used, with speed of resolution being a critical factor. Shield reports faster execution, fewer failures and fewer timeouts. Its teams also spend less time writing detailed instructions to an agent or helping it through a task. Shield is testing remote-desktop workflows that would let agents perform more complex actions directly on a computer’s desktop. Jain says, “With GPT‑6 Astra, Forge is now truly an extension of our human technicians.” Product updates, practical guides, upcoming events, and more. articles.title: Nauru’s president has no political opponents after all lawmakers joined the government side
articles.content: WELLINGTON, New Zealand (AP) — Nauru’s president, David Adeang, has said all opposition lawmakers in parliament have joined his government, a move he said reflected “unity, stability and shared purpose” in the Pacific Island country’s politics. The unusual move leaves the 19-member parliament without any political opposition. While it’s common for island countries in the South Pacific Ocean to take fluid approaches to forming government and opposition blocs or for lawmakers to switch between them, political debate is habitually robust and Nauru is rare in having no opposing politicians at all. In a Facebook post Tuesday, Adeang didn’t explain what had prompted the change beyond a “shared commitment” to put Nauru’s interests first. He also didn’t suggest who would supply the scrutiny usually provided by opponents in a country with a single house of parliament. “There will still be a diversity of views and robust debate as in any strong and healthy democracy,” Adeang wrote. The appointment of two lawmakers, Pyon Deiye and Jason Bingham Agir, as deputy cabinet ministers meant that Nauru’s parliament was in total support of the government for the first time since the country’s independence in 1968, Adeang said. Government Facebook posts announcing the change were the sole source of information about it; all news outlets in the country of 12,000 people are government-owned. Foreign reporters are discouraged from traveling there, with journalist visa applications priced at 8,000 Australian dollars ($5,445). Adeang made global news headlines in August when he said his country would officially become known as Naoero, making it the latest state to formally adopt the local spelling of its name. It brought international attention to a country visited by few. Nauru, a constitutional republic and United Nations member, is one of the world’s smallest countries by both population and size. Limited infrastructure, a remote location and the environmental damage wrought by phosphate mining mean it attracts few visitors, unlike many other Pacific islands where foreign tourism is the main economic driver. But it’s among the South Pacific countries where domestic politics have drawn keener outside interest in recent years as the sprawling ocean where Nauru is located has become the site of geopolitical contest between major powers. The potentially wealthy exclusive economic zones surrounding some of the poorest Pacific nations and the strategic importance of their locations in times of global volatility have provoked a race between China and Western countries with interests in the region to win influence with governments there. Nauru is no exception. In 2024, it was one of a dwindling number of countries to hold diplomatic relations with Taipei, but severed them in order to resume ties with Beijing, which holds that Taiwan is part of China. It’s become one of Beijing’s warmest allies in the region since. Australia in turn signed a lucrative pact with Adeang later in 2024 in which Nauru promised Canberra veto power over any security deals with Beijing. Adeang’s government said Friday that the president had arrived in China for meetings with officials, accompanied by other lawmakers including newly appointed cabinet members Deiye and Agir. The president has led the country since 2023 when a no-confidence motion ousted his predecessor. He was chosen unopposed to continue in the job among lawmakers sworn in after the 2025 election. In 2014, then Justice Minister Adeang suspended opposition lawmakers from Parliament for remarks they made to international news outlets. Most lawmakers in Nauru run as independents and don’t belong to political parties, which is common in Pacific Island countries. Freedom House, a Washington-based organization that promotes democracy, said in its 2026 report that Nauru’s people “generally enjoy political rights and civil liberties” but that corruption was “an ongoing challenge.” The country was one of the world’s richest per capita at the height of phosphate exports but the economy plummeted when the industry collapsed. Nauru experimented with a golden passport scheme and became a tax haven for a period. It now subsists on foreign aid, sales of tuna fisheries licenses in its waters and funding from Australia first to host that country’s offshore detention facilities for asylum seekers and later to accommodate foreign criminals Australia wanted to deport.
